Variational Approach to Optimal IPS Estimator for Multi-logger Off-Policy Evaluation

Joon Suk Huh ††thanks: These authors contributed equally to this work. Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: University of Wisconsin–Madison, USA Email: joon@cs.wisc.edu    Junghoon Seo11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: PIT IN Corp., Republic of Korea Email: sjh@pitin-ev.com
Abstract

We study off-policy evaluation (OPE) in contextual bandits with data collected from multiple logging policies. Inverse propensity scoring (IPS) is a standard approach to OPE and extends naturally to the multi-logger setting. However, as highlighted by Agarwal et al. (2017), neither balanced nor weighted IPS consistently outperforms the other in this setting. We resolve this dilemma by deriving an optimal IPS estimator with sample-dependent weights that minimize variance subject to unbiasedness. Using a variational calculus approach, we obtain closed-form optimal weights, yielding an estimator that is unbiased and achieves asymptotically optimal variance within a generalized weighted-IPS estimator class. Instead of a reward model, the estimator needs only a K×KK\times K matrix and a KK-vector of moments, where KK is the number of logging policies, and we quantify how much efficiency this costs relative to the semiparametric oracle. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that our estimator generally improves on existing multi-logger IPS methods. We also extend our estimator to a doubly robust form by incorporating a conditional reward estimator. We compare the resulting DR extension with the semiparametrically efficient DR estimator of Kallus et al. (2021), both theoretically and empirically. We show that the two estimators achieve the same asymptotic variance when the conditional reward estimator is consistent, while our estimator can retain semiparametric efficiency under certain forms of reward misspecification. Empirically, the proposed DR estimator often achieves lower estimation error than the existing DR baseline.

1 Introduction

Off-policy evaluation (OPE) is a core tool for data-driven decision making, with applications in recommender systems, healthcare, and advertising. The goal is to estimate the value of an evaluation policy using data collected by one or more different logging policies. While the single-logger setting is well understood, many practical datasets are collected from multiple logging policies, for example through heterogeneous systems, parallel deployments, or sequential changes to a production policy (Agarwal et al., 2017; Saito et al., 2021; Jung and Bellot, 2024). This multi-logger structure creates a basic statistical challenge: different strata can have very different overlaps with the evaluation policy, so combining them poorly can lead to large variance.

Inverse propensity scoring (IPS) is a standard approach to OPE (Rosenbaum and Rubin, 1983; Precup et al., 2000; Bottou et al., 2013). In the single-logger case, IPS reweights each observed reward by the propensity ratio between the evaluation and logging policies. In the multi-logger case, however, there is an additional design choice: one must decide how much each logger should contribute to the final estimate. Existing approaches answer this question in different ways. Naive IPS treats all logged samples with their own propensity ratios, balanced IPS uses the sample-size-weighted average logging policy, and weighted IPS chooses logger-level weights based on estimated variances (Agarwal et al., 2017). As observed by Agarwal et al. (2017), the relative performance of balanced and weighted IPS is highly instance dependent: neither consistently dominates the other across problem instances, and naive IPS is dominated in their analysis. Kallus et al. (2021) later characterized the semiparametrically efficient estimator over a broader class, which serves as our benchmark.

We revisit this problem from a variational perspective. Instead of choosing among a fixed set of IPS estimators, we consider a generalized weighted-IPS class ΓwIPS\Gamma_{\mathrm{wIPS}} in which each sample may receive a weight depending on the logged tuple and its logger identity. That is, the weights are functions of the state, action, reward, and logger. We impose constraints that ensure unbiasedness and then directly minimize the variance functional over all feasible weight functions. This yields a convex variance minimization problem whose solution admits a closed-form characterization. The resulting estimator, denoted J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}, can be viewed as a balanced-IPS estimator augmented with an optimal control-variate term built from the logging propensities. This construction does not require the conditional mean reward. Instead, it estimates a K×KK\times K matrix 𝐓\mathbf{T} and a vector 𝐜∈ℝK\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} of moments (§3).

This perspective clarifies the apparent instance-dependence of existing IPS estimators. The optimal weights depend on the interaction among the evaluation policy, the logging policies, the reward distribution, and the stratum sizes. Thus, fixed IPS rules such as naive IPS, balanced IPS, and weighted IPS can each perform well on some instances and poorly on others. By optimizing over a class containing these IPS baselines, J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} adapts to the instance and achieves the smallest asymptotic variance within ΓwIPS\Gamma_{\mathrm{wIPS}}. We prove that the corresponding feasible cross-fitted implementation is unbiased when logging policies are known and is asymptotically normal with the optimal variance.

We also relate our estimator to the semiparametric efficiency theory of Kallus et al. (2021). Their framework shows that the most efficient estimator uses the conditional mean reward as a control variate. Our IPS estimator can be viewed as a restricted, reward model-free version of this idea: instead of estimating the conditional mean reward directly, it constructs the best control variate available from the logging policies. When this logger-induced control variate is rich enough to represent the relevant reward structure, our estimator asymptotically recovers the efficient oracle. Otherwise, its excess variance is determined by the part of the reward structure that cannot be represented by the logging policies.

Finally, we extend our variational approach to a doubly robust estimator, denoted J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}}, by incorporating a reward model. This extension keeps the same idea as our IPS estimator: it uses the logging policies to choose an additional variance-reducing correction. This makes it directly comparable to the doubly robust balanced IPS estimator J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}} of Kallus et al. (2021). When the reward model is correctly specified, both estimators attain the same asymptotic variance. When the reward model is misspecified, however, J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} can remain efficient if the misspecification is representable by the logging policies, whereas J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}} need not. This gives our DR extension an additional robustness advantage.

Summary of Contributions.

We make the following contributions:

  1. 1.

    A variationally optimal IPS estimator for multi-logger OPE. We introduce a generalized weighted-IPS class ΓwIPS\Gamma_{\mathrm{wIPS}} and derive the variance-minimizing unbiased estimator within this class. The resulting estimator J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} has closed-form sample-dependent weights and estimates 𝐓\mathbf{T} and 𝐜\mathbf{c} in place of a reward model.

  2. 2.

    Closed-form characterization, feasible estimation, and projection interpretation. We show that the optimal weights are characterized by a linear system 𝐓​𝜶=𝐜\mathbf{T}\bm{\alpha}=\mathbf{c}, whose components can be estimated from data, leading to a practical cross-fitted implementation. We further show that this system has a geometric interpretation: it projects the reward-weighted evaluation policy onto the span of the logging policies, and the resulting projection residual exactly determines the variance gap to the semiparametrically efficient oracle.

  3. 3.

    Doubly robust extension and comparison with efficient DR estimators. We extend J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} to a doubly robust estimator J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} by applying the same variational construction to residuals based on q^\hat{q}. We show that J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} matches the asymptotic variance of J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}} when q^\hat{q} is consistent, and can retain the oracle variance under certain structured misspecifications of q^\hat{q}.

  4. 4.

    Empirical validation. Across benchmark datasets and a broad range of logger mixtures, our IPS estimator generally improves over existing multi-logger IPS baselines. The doubly robust extension also often achieves lower estimation error than the semiparametrically efficient baseline.

Related Work.

Appendix G discusses related work on OPE with multiple loggers (He et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020), connections to multiple importance sampling (Veach and Guibas, 1995; Elvira et al., 2019; Kondapaneni et al., 2019), and broader variance-reduction methods for IPS.

2.1 Problem Setting

We study OPE in contextual bandits, following the multi-logger setup in (Agarwal et al., 2017; He et al., 2019; Kallus et al., 2021). A policy π\pi maps a state (i.e., context) s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} to a distribution over actions in 𝒜\mathcal{A}, written as π⁡(a∣s)\pi(a\mid s).

An environment is defined by the following unknown distributions: a context distribution ps​(s)p_{s}(s) and reward distributions pr​(r∣s,a)p_{r}(r\mid s,a) over ℛ⊆ℝ\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathbb{R} for each context-action pair (s,a)∈𝒮×𝒜(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}. Interaction proceeds as follows: the environment samples S∼psS\sim p_{s}, the actor samples A∼π(⋅∣S)A\sim\pi(\,\cdot\mid S), and the environment then samples the reward R∼pr(⋅∣S,A)R\sim p_{r}(\,\cdot\mid S,\,A). This induces a joint distribution μπ\mu_{\pi} on 𝒮×𝒜×ℛ\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{R}, whose density is ps​(s)​π​(a|s)​pr​(r|s,a)p_{s}(s)\,\pi(a|s)\,p_{r}(r|s,a) with respect to the dominating measure μ⁡(d​s,d​a,d​r)=μs​(d​s)​μa​(d​a)​μr​(d​r∣s,a)\mu(ds,da,dr)=\mu_{s}(ds)\,\mu_{a}(da)\,\mu_{r}(dr\mid s,a), where μr(⋅∣s,a)\mu_{r}(\cdot\mid s,a) is a reference kernel on ℛ\mathcal{R}. Equivalently, μπ​(d​s,d​a,d​r)=PS​(d​s)​π​(d​a∣s)​PR​(d​r∣s,a)\mu_{\pi}(ds,da,dr)=P_{S}(ds)\,\pi(da\mid s)\,P_{R}(dr\mid s,a), where PS​(d​s)=ps​(s)​μs​(d​s)P_{S}(ds)=p_{s}(s)\,\mu_{s}(ds), π⁡(d​a∣s)=π⁡(a∣s)​μa​(d​a)\pi(da\mid s)=\pi(a\mid s)\,\mu_{a}(da), and PR​(d​r∣s,a)=pr​(r∣s,a)​μr​(d​r∣s,a)P_{R}(dr\mid s,a)=p_{r}(r\mid s,a)\,\mu_{r}(dr\mid s,a). The expected reward of the policy π\pi, denoted J⁡(π)J(\pi), is

J​(π)≔𝔼μπ​[R],\displaystyle J(\pi)\coloneq\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi}}[R],

where 𝔼μπ\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi}} denotes expectation with respect to μπ\mu_{\pi}.

The goal of OPE is to estimate the policy value J⁡(πe)J(\pi_{e}) of an evaluation policy πe\pi_{e} from logged data. In the single-logger case, we observe i.i.d. samples 𝒟≔{(Sj,Aj,Rj)}j=1n\mathcal{D}\coloneq\big\{(S_{j},A_{j},R_{j})\big\}_{j=1}^{n} drawn from μπ\mu_{\pi}, where π\pi is the logging policy and typically π≠πe\pi\neq\,\pi_{e}. In this work, we consider stratified OPE with multiple logging policies (πi)i∈[K](\pi_{i})_{i\in[K]}. The full dataset is 𝒟≔{𝒟i}i∈[K]\mathcal{D}\coloneq\{\mathcal{D}_{i}\}_{i\in[K]}, where the strata are independent and each stratum 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i} consists of nin_{i} i.i.d. samples from μπi\mu_{\pi_{i}}, namely 𝒟i≔{(Si​j,Ai​j,Ri​j)}j=1ni\mathcal{D}_{i}\coloneq\big\{(S_{ij},A_{ij},R_{ij})\big\}_{j=1}^{n_{i}}, where Si​j∼psS_{ij}\sim p_{s}, Ai​j∼πi(⋅∣Si​j)A_{ij}\sim\pi_{i}(\cdot\mid S_{ij}), and Ri​j∼pr(⋅∣Si​j,Ai​j)R_{ij}\sim p_{r}(\cdot\mid S_{ij},A_{ij}).

2.2 Existing Inverse Propensity Scoring (IPS)-based Approaches

Naive IPS.

Naive IPS reweights each observed reward by the propensity ratio between the evaluation and logging policies:

J^IPS​(πe,𝒟)=1n​∑i=1K∑(S,A,R)∈𝒟iR​πe​(A∣S)πi​(A∣S),\displaystyle\hat{J}_{\mathrm{IPS}}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\sum_{(S,A,R)\in\mathcal{D}_{i}}R\,\frac{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{i}(A\mid S)}, (2.1)

where n≔∑i=1Knin\coloneq\sum_{i=1}^{K}n_{i} is the total number of samples.

Balanced IPS.

Agarwal et al. (2017) proposed a multiple importance sampling (MIS)-inspired estimator that uses the averaged logging policy as inverse propensity score:

J^bIPS​(πe,𝒟)=1n​∑i=1K∑(S,A,R)∈𝒟iR​πe​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S),\displaystyle\hat{J}_{\mathrm{bIPS}}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\sum_{(S,A,R)\in\mathcal{D}_{i}}R\,\frac{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}, (2.2)

where πavg≔1n​∑i=1Kni​πi\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}\coloneq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{K}n_{i}\,\pi_{i} and ni≔|𝒟i|n_{i}\coloneq|\mathcal{D}_{i}|.

Weighted IPS.

Agarwal et al. (2017) also introduced weighted IPS, which combines logger-specific IPS estimates using variance-based weights:

J^wIPS​(πe,𝒟)=∑i=1Kγ^i​∑(S,A,R)∈𝒟iR​πe​(A∣S)πi​(A∣S),\displaystyle\hat{J}_{\mathrm{wIPS}}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})=\sum^{K}_{i=1}\hat{\gamma}_{i}\,\sum_{(S,A,R)\in\mathcal{D}_{i}}R\,\frac{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{i}(A\mid S)}, (2.3)

where γ^i≔(σ^r2(πe||πi)∑j=1Knjσ^r2(πe||πj))−1\hat{\gamma}_{i}\coloneq\left(\widehat{\sigma}_{r}^{2}(\pi_{e}||\pi_{i})\sum^{K}_{j=1}\frac{n_{j}}{\widehat{\sigma}_{r}^{2}(\pi_{e}||\pi_{j})}\right)^{-1} and σ^r2(πe||πi)\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{r}(\pi_{e}||\pi_{i}) is a positive consistent estimator of Varμπi​[R​πe​(A∣S)πi​(A∣S)]\mathrm{Var}_{\mu_{\pi_{i}}}\!\left[R\,\frac{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{i}(A\mid S)}\right], which quantifies the divergence between the target and logging policies.

Doubly Robust Balanced IPS.

Kallus et al. (2021) proposed a doubly robust version of J^bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{bIPS}} using a conditional mean reward estimator q^\hat{q}:

J^DR​-​bIPS​(πe,𝒟)=1n​∑i=1K∑(S,A,R)∈𝒟i[πe​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S)​(R−q^​(S,A))+q^​(S,πe)],\displaystyle\hat{J}_{{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}}}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\sum_{(S,A,R)\in\mathcal{D}_{i}}\left[\frac{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}\big(R-\hat{q}(S,A)\big)+\hat{q}(S,\pi_{e})\right], (2.4)

where q^​(S,πe)≔∫𝒜q^​(S,a)​πe​(a∣S)​d​μa​(a)\hat{q}(S,\pi_{e})\coloneq\int_{\mathcal{A}}\hat{q}(S,a)\pi_{e}(a\mid S)\,d\mu_{a}(a). When the logging policies are known and q^\hat{q} consistently estimates the conditional mean reward q(s,a)≔𝔼[R∣S=s,A=a]q(s,a)\coloneq\mathbb{E}[R\mid S=s,A=a], J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}}} attains the semiparametric efficiency bound within the estimator class studied by Kallus et al. (2021), under their regularity conditions. In practice, q^\hat{q} is estimated by cross-fitting: the reward model is trained on one part of the data and evaluated on held-out samples. The same cross-fitting strategy for nuisance quantities is also used in J^wIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{wIPS}}.

3 Variational Optimization Approach

In this section, we introduce our main estimator, which is derived by optimizing a convex variance functional and is asymptotically optimal within the generalized weighted-IPS class denoted by ΓwIPS\Gamma_{\mathrm{wIPS}}.

3.1 Generalized Weighted-IPS Estimator Class

Let 𝐰≔(wi)i∈[K]\mathbf{w}\coloneq(w_{i})_{i\in[K]}, where each wi:𝒮×𝒜×ℛ→ℝw_{i}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{R}\to\mathbb{R} is a sample-dependent weight function. The generalized weighted-IPS estimator class ΓwIPS\Gamma_{\mathrm{wIPS}} is

J^​(πe,𝐰,𝒟)≔∑i=1K1ni​∑(S,A,R)∈𝒟iwi​(S,A,R)​πe​(A∣S)πi​(A∣S)\displaystyle\boxed{\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\mathbf{w};\mathcal{D})\coloneq\sum^{K}_{i=1}\frac{1}{n_{i}}\sum_{(S,A,R)\in\mathcal{D}_{i}}w_{i}(S,A,R)\,\frac{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{i}(A\mid S)}} (3.1)

Estimators in ΓwIPS\Gamma_{\mathrm{wIPS}} are unbiased when the weights satisfy the following conditions for every ω=(s,a,r)\omega=(s,a,r):

Normalization:∑i=1Kwi(ω)=ρr(ω),Dominance:πi(a|s)=0⟹wi(s,a,r)=0.\displaystyle\textbf{Normalization:}\ \sum_{i=1}^{K}w_{i}(\omega)=\rho_{r}(\omega),\quad\textbf{Dominance:}\ \pi_{i}(a|s)=0\implies w_{i}(s,a,r)=0.
Theorem 3.1.

[Unbiasedness] For any weights 𝐰∈(L2)K\mathbf{w}\in(L^{2})^{K} that satisfy the normalization and dominance conditions and for which each weighted score wi​(S,A,R)​πe​(A∣S)/πi​(A∣S)w_{i}(S,A,R)\,\pi_{e}(A\mid S)/\pi_{i}(A\mid S) is μπi\mu_{\pi_{i}}-integrable, J^​(πe,𝐰,𝒟)\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\mathbf{w};\mathcal{D}) is unbiased, that is, J⁡(πe)=𝔼⁡[J^​(πe,𝐰,𝒟)]J(\pi_{e})=\mathbb{E}[\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\mathbf{w};\mathcal{D})], where the expectation is over the sampling randomness of logged data 𝒟≔(𝒟i)i∈[K]\mathcal{D}\coloneq(\mathcal{D}_{i})_{i\in[K]}.

In §4.3, we compare ΓwIPS\Gamma_{\mathrm{wIPS}} with the broader class of Kallus et al. (2021), whose efficient estimator requires an estimate of the conditional mean reward.

Variationally Optimized Weights.

Since J^​(πe,𝐰,𝒟)\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\mathbf{w};\mathcal{D}) is a linear functional of 𝐰\mathbf{w}, its variance is convex. We optimize this variance functional directly over feasible 𝐰\mathbf{w} satisfying the normalization and dominance constraints. The resulting optimal weight vector 𝐰⋆≔(wi⋆)i∈[K]\mathbf{w}^{\star}\coloneq(w_{i}^{\star})_{i\in[K]}, whose optimality is established in Theorem 4.1, takes the form

wi⋆​(s,a,r)=αi⋆​πi​(a|s)πe​(a|s)+ni​πi​(a|s)n​πavg​(a|s)​(r−∑j=1Kαj⋆​πj​(a|s)πe​(a|s))\displaystyle w^{\star}_{i}(s,a,r)=\frac{\alpha^{\star}_{i}\pi_{i}(a|s)}{\pi_{e}(a|s)}+\frac{n_{i}\,\pi_{i}(a|s)}{n\,\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(a|s)}\left(r-\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\!\alpha^{\star}_{j}\,\pi_{j}(a|s)}{\pi_{e}(a|s)}\right) (3.2)

where 𝜶⋆≔(αi⋆)i∈[K]\bm{\alpha}^{\star}\coloneq(\alpha^{\star}_{i})_{i\in[K]} is a solution of 𝐓​𝜶=𝐜\mathbf{T}\bm{\alpha}=\mathbf{c}, with 𝐓∈ℝK×K\mathbf{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times K} and 𝐜∈ℝK\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} whose components are given by

Ti​j≔𝔼μπi​[πj​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S)],ci≔𝔼μπi​[R​πe​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S)]\displaystyle T_{ij}\coloneq\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{i}}}\!\left[\frac{\pi_{j}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}\right],\ \ c_{i}\coloneq\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{i}}}\!\left[R\,\frac{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}\right] (3.3)

We call 𝐓\mathbf{T} the technique matrix and 𝐜\mathbf{c} the contribution vector. Estimating 𝐓\mathbf{T} and 𝐜\mathbf{c} thus replaces estimating the conditional mean reward function. We later show in this section that the equation 𝐓​𝜶=𝐜\mathbf{T}\bm{\alpha}=\mathbf{c} can be interpreted as the normal equation for an orthogonal projection.

Control-Variate Form.

Plugging the expression for 𝐰⋆\mathbf{w}^{\star} in (3.2) into J^​(πe,𝐰⋆,𝒟)\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\mathbf{w}^{\star};\mathcal{D}) in (3.1) yields the following form of the variationally optimal IPS estimator 11 1 With a slight abuse of notation, we write J^​(πe,𝜶⋆,𝒟)=J^​(πe,𝐰⋆,𝒟)\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\bm{\alpha}^{\star};\mathcal{D})=\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\mathbf{w}^{\star};\mathcal{D}).:

J^​(πe,𝜶⋆,𝒟)=1n​∑i=1K∑(S,A,R)∈𝒟i[R​πe​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S)+∑k=1Kαk⋆−g𝜶⋆​(S,A)πavg​(A∣S)]\displaystyle\boxed{\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\bm{\alpha}^{\star};\mathcal{D})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\sum_{(S,A,R)\in\mathcal{D}_{i}}\Bigg[\,\frac{R\,\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\alpha^{\star}_{k}-\frac{g_{\bm{\alpha}^{\star}}(S,A)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}\Bigg]} (3.4)

where g𝜶⋆​(s,a)≔∑k∈[K]αk⋆​πk​(a|s)g_{\bm{\alpha}^{\star}}(s,a)\coloneq\sum_{k\in[K]}\alpha^{\star}_{k}\,\pi_{k}(a|s). We refer to this as the control-variate form: the term involving ∑kαk⋆−g𝜶⋆/πavg\sum_{k}\alpha_{k}^{\star}-g_{\bm{\alpha}^{\star}}/\pi_{\mathrm{avg}} is mean-zero and therefore acts as a control variate.

Geometric View.

Let q(s,a)≔𝔼[R|S=s,A=a]q(s,a)\coloneq\mathbb{E}[R\,|\,S=s,A=a] denote the conditional mean reward. Then, we can view g𝜶⋆g_{\bm{\alpha}^{\star}} as the orthogonal projection of q​πeq\,\pi_{e} onto the finite-dimensional space spanned by {πi}i∈[K]\{\pi_{i}\}_{i\in[K]}. Specifically, consider L2​(μlog,𝒮×𝒜)L^{2}(\mu_{\log},\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}), where μlog\mu_{\log} is given by

d​μlog​(s,a)≔ps​(s)πavg​(a|s)​d​μs,a​(s,a),\displaystyle d\mu_{\log}(s,a)\coloneq\frac{p_{s}(s)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(a|s)}\,d\mu_{s,a}(s,a),

with μs,a=μs⊗μa\mu_{s,a}=\mu_{s}\otimes\mu_{a} denoting the base measure over 𝒮×𝒜\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}. Equip L2​(𝒮×𝒜,μlog)L^{2}(\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A},\mu_{\log}) with the inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩μlog\left\langle\cdot,\cdot\right\rangle_{\mu_{\log}}. Then, one can rewrite (3.3) in terms of ⟨⋅,⋅⟩μlog\left\langle\cdot,\cdot\right\rangle_{\mu_{\log}} as

Ti​j=⟨πi,πj⟩μlog,ci=⟨q​πe,πi⟩μlog.\displaystyle T_{ij}=\big\langle\pi_{i},\pi_{j}\big\rangle_{\mu_{\log}},\quad c_{i}=\big\langle q\,\pi_{e},\pi_{i}\big\rangle_{\mu_{\log}}.

Thus, 𝐓​𝜶⋆=𝐜\mathbf{T}\bm{\alpha}^{\star}=\mathbf{c} if and only if ⟨q​πe−∑jαj⋆​πj,πi⟩μlog=0\big\langle q\,\pi_{e}-\sum_{j}\alpha^{\star}_{j}\pi_{j},\pi_{i}\big\rangle_{\mu_{\log}}=0 for all i∈[K]i\in[K]. This shows that g𝜶⋆g_{\bm{\alpha}^{\star}} is the projection of q​πeq\,\pi_{e} onto span⁡({πi}i∈[K])\mathrm{span}\big(\{\pi_{i}\}_{i\in[K]}\big), with respect to the norm induced by ⟨⋅,⋅⟩μlog\left\langle\cdot,\cdot\right\rangle_{\mu_{\log}}.

We formally state this observation in Lemma E.2. Later, in §4.3, we relate the squared ∥⋅∥μlog\|\cdot\|_{\mu_{\log}} norm of the residual component of q​πeq\,\pi_{e} orthogonal to span⁡({πi}i∈[K])\mathrm{span}\big(\{\pi_{i}\}_{i\in[K]}\big) to the excess variance of our estimator relative to the semiparametrically efficient oracle of Kallus et al. (2021).

3.2 Feasible Variationally Optimal Estimator J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}

In this section, we derive a feasible variationally optimal estimator J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}. Specifically, we employ the logger-wise cross-fitting strategy (Zheng and van der Laan, 2011; Chernozhukov et al., 2018; Kallus et al., 2021): one part of the data is used to estimate the nuisance parameter 𝜶\bm{\alpha} by estimating 𝐓\mathbf{T} and 𝐜\mathbf{c}, while the other part is used to compute the estimator (3.4).

Computing J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}.

For each i∈[K]i\in[K], let {𝒟i(z)}z∈[Z]\big\{\mathcal{D}^{(z)}_{i}\big\}_{z\in[Z]} be a ZZ-fold partition (Z≥2Z\geq 2) of 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i} into nonempty folds chosen independently of the observed values, with 𝒟i(−z)≔𝒟i∖𝒟i(z)\mathcal{D}^{(-z)}_{i}\coloneq\mathcal{D}_{i}\setminus\mathcal{D}_{i}^{(z)} and ni(−z)≔|𝒟i(−z)|n_{i}^{(-z)}\coloneq\big|\mathcal{D}_{i}^{(-z)}\big|. Then, for each fold z∈[Z]z\in[Z], estimate 𝐓,𝐜\mathbf{T},\mathbf{c} by

T^i​j(z)≔1ni(−z)​∑(S,A,R)∈𝒟i(−z)πj​(A∣S)πavg(−z)​(A∣S),c^i(z)≔1ni(−z)​∑(S,A,R)∈𝒟i(−z)R​πe​(A∣S)πavg(−z)​(A∣S)\displaystyle\hat{T}_{ij}^{(z)}\coloneq\frac{1}{n_{i}^{(-z)}}\sum_{(S,A,R)\in\mathcal{D}_{i}^{(-z)}}\frac{\pi_{j}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}^{(-z)}(A\mid S)},\quad\hat{c}_{i}^{(z)}\coloneq\frac{1}{n_{i}^{(-z)}}\sum_{(S,A,R)\in\mathcal{D}_{i}^{(-z)}}\frac{R\,\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}^{(-z)}(A\mid S)} (3.5)

where πavg(−z)≔1n(−z)​∑i∈[K]ni(−z)​πi\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}^{(-z)}\coloneq\frac{1}{n^{(-z)}}\sum_{i\in[K]}n_{i}^{(-z)}\pi_{i} with n(−z)≔∑i∈[K]ni(−z)n^{(-z)}\coloneq\sum_{i\in[K]}n_{i}^{(-z)}. Then, we estimate 𝜶⋆\bm{\alpha}^{\star} with 𝜶^(z)≔(𝐓^(z))†​𝐜^(z)\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)}\coloneq\big(\hat{\mathbf{T}}^{(z)}\big)^{\dagger}\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{(z)}, where †\dagger denotes the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse.

Let ni(z)≔|𝒟i(z)|n_{i}^{(z)}\coloneq\big|\mathcal{D}_{i}^{(z)}\big| and n(z)≔∑i∈[K]ni(z)n^{(z)}\coloneq\sum_{i\in[K]}n^{(z)}_{i}. Then, the feasible variationally optimal estimator is

J^oIPS​(πe,𝒟)≔1n​∑z=1Zn(z)​J^​(πe,𝜶^(z),𝒟(z))\displaystyle\boxed{\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})\coloneq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{z=1}^{Z}n^{(z)}\hat{J}\big(\pi_{e},\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)};\mathcal{D}^{(z)}\big)} (3.6)

where J^​(πe,𝜶^(z),𝒟(z))\hat{J}\left(\pi_{e},\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)};\mathcal{D}^{(z)}\right) is (3.4) evaluated with 𝜶^(z)\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)} and 𝒟(z)≔{𝒟i(z)}i∈[K]\mathcal{D}^{(z)}\coloneq\big\{\mathcal{D}_{i}^{(z)}\big\}_{i\in[K]} in place of 𝜶⋆\bm{\alpha}^{\star} and 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Note that the quantity πavg\pi_{\mathrm{avg}} in (3.4) depends on 𝒟\mathcal{D} through ni/nn_{i}/n, so it is also replaced with πavg(z)≔1n(z)​∑i∈[K]ni(z)​πi\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}^{(z)}\coloneq\frac{1}{n^{(z)}}\sum_{i\in[K]}n_{i}^{(z)}\pi_{i}.

When Logging Policies are Unknown.

When the logging policies are unknown, we plug consistent estimators of πi​(a|s)\pi_{i}(a|s) and πavg​(a|s)\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(a|s) into the above procedure. The estimation procedures are given in Appendix A.

In Theorem 4.2, we show that J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} is unbiased and asymptotically normal with the optimal asymptotic variance n​Var​[J^​(πe,𝐰⋆,𝒟)]n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\mathbf{w}^{\star};\mathcal{D})] when the logging policies are known; Remark 2 discusses estimated logging policies.

4 Theoretical Analysis

In this section, we analyze J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} introduced in §3 and prove its asymptotic variance optimality within the generalized weighted-IPS class (3.1). We then compare J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} with other estimators, including the estimator J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}} (2.4), which is asymptotically optimal within a class containing the three IPS baselines (Kallus et al., 2021) but requires an estimator of the conditional mean reward. We characterize the variance gap between J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} and J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}} in terms of the residual from projecting the evaluation policy πe\pi_{e}, weighted by the conditional mean reward q⁡(s,a)q(s,a), namely q​πeq\,\pi_{e}, onto the logger basis space.

For simplicity of the analysis, we make the following assumptions.

Assumption 1 (Regularity).
  1. (i)

    All logging and evaluation policies have strictly positive densities over the action space at every state in the support of psp_{s}.22 2 Consequently, we drop the dominance condition in the variance minimization problem, but our solution still satisfies it.

  2. (ii)

    The weighted scores wi​(S,A,R)​πe​(A∣S)/πi​(A∣S)w_{i}(S,A,R)\,\pi_{e}(A\mid S)/\pi_{i}(A\mid S) have finite second moments under μπi\mu_{\pi_{i}}, and the optimal weights in (3.2) are square-integrable.

  3. (iii)

    For the feasible estimator, KK and ZZ are fixed and the folds of each stratum have equal sizes up to rounding. For every i∈[K]i\in[K] and z∈[Z]z\in[Z], the summand of (3.4) computed with 𝜶^(z)\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)} converges in probability to the summand computed with 𝜶⋆\bm{\alpha}^{\star} in L2​(μπi)L^{2}(\mu_{\pi_{i}}), and both summands have finite second moments, including over the randomness of the training folds.

Remark 1.

If πe\pi_{e} has zeros, as for the deterministic evaluation policy in §5, Assumption 1(i) fails: the weights (3.2) are undefined where πe​(a∣s)=0\pi_{e}(a\mid s)=0, and the control-variate form (3.4) is no longer a member of ΓwIPS\Gamma_{\mathrm{wIPS}}. The control-variate form remains unbiased for every 𝛂\bm{\alpha}, and any solution of 𝐓​𝛂=𝐜\mathbf{T}\bm{\alpha}=\mathbf{c} still minimizes its variance over 𝛂∈ℝK\bm{\alpha}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}. The comparisons in §4.3 extend to such πe\pi_{e} by continuity, by applying them to πeϵ≔(1−ϵ)​πe+ϵ​πu\pi_{e}^{\epsilon}\coloneq(1-\epsilon)\pi_{e}+\epsilon\pi_{u}, where πu\pi_{u} is the uniform policy, and letting ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0.

4.1 Derivation of Optimal Weights

Let J^​(πe,𝐰,𝒟)\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\mathbf{w};\mathcal{D}) be a generalized weighted-IPS estimator (3.1). Then, Var​[J^​(πe,𝐰,𝒟)]\mathrm{Var}\big[\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\mathbf{w};\mathcal{D})\big] is a convex functional of 𝐰\mathbf{w}, so the variance can be optimized directly over the feasible weights. The main convex program of interest is

minimize𝐰∈(L2)K\displaystyle\underset{\mathbf{w}\in(L^{2})^{K}}{\text{minimize}} Var​[J^​(πe,𝐰,𝒟)]\displaystyle\hskip-36.135pt\mathrm{Var}\big[\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\mathbf{w};\mathcal{D})\big] (4.1)
subject to ∑i=1Kwi​(ω)=ρr​(ω),∀ω∈supp⁡(μπe),\displaystyle\hskip-36.135pt\sum^{K}_{i=1}w_{i}(\omega)=\rho_{r}(\omega),\quad\forall\omega\in\mathrm{supp}\,(\mu_{\pi_{e}}),
Theorem 4.1.

The weight vector 𝐰⋆\mathbf{w}^{\star} given in (3.2) solves the variance minimization problem (4.1).

The proof of this theorem is given in Appendix E.2.

By Theorem 4.1, computing J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} only requires estimating 𝐓\mathbf{T} and 𝐜\mathbf{c}, whose ii-th rows are averages over stratum ii, and then solving the K×KK\times K system 𝐓​𝜶=𝐜\mathbf{T}\bm{\alpha}=\mathbf{c} for each fold. Assuming each propensity evaluation takes constant time, accumulating the moments takes O⁡(n​K)O(nK) time and each solve takes O⁡(K3)O(K^{3}), so ZZ-fold cross-fitting costs O⁡(Z⁡(n​K+K3))O(Z(nK+K^{3})), which is O⁡(n​K+K3)O(nK+K^{3}) for fixed ZZ. If the per-fold moments are accumulated in one pass over the data, the extra memory is O⁡(Z​K2)O(ZK^{2}), and a second pass evaluates the estimator; storing every cross-logger propensity instead takes O⁡(n​K)O(nK). These counts exclude fitting nuisance models such as propensity models. Appendix F reports the corresponding runtimes.

4.2 Unbiasedness and Asymptotic Variance Optimality of J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} within ΓwIPS\Gamma_{\mathrm{wIPS}}

We next analyze the feasible cross-fitted estimator J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}. Specifically, we prove its unbiasedness and asymptotic variance optimality within the generalized weighted-IPS estimator class ΓwIPS\Gamma_{\mathrm{wIPS}}. We follow the multi-logger asymptotic regime of Kallus et al. (2021): for each logger, the number of observations is ni′=m​nin^{\prime}_{i}=mn_{i}, and we consider the limit m→∞m\to\infty.

Theorem 4.2.

Let n′≔∑i=1Kni′n^{\prime}\coloneq\sum_{i=1}^{K}n^{\prime}_{i} with ni′≔m​nin^{\prime}_{i}\coloneq mn_{i}. Under Assumption 1, when the logging policies are known, J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} is unbiased, and

n′​(J^oIPS​(πe,𝒟)−J⁡(πe))​→𝑑​𝒩​(0,n​Var​[J^​(πe,𝐰⋆,𝒟)])\displaystyle\sqrt{n^{\prime}}\left(\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})-J(\pi_{e})\right)\overset{d}{\to}\mathcal{N}\left(0,n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\mathbf{w}^{\star};\mathcal{D})]\right)

as m→∞m\to\infty, where n≔∑i=1Knin\coloneq\sum_{i=1}^{K}n_{i} and Var⁡[J^​(πe,𝐰⋆,𝒟)]\mathrm{Var}[\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\mathbf{w}^{\star};\mathcal{D})] is computed at the base stratum sizes (ni)i=1K(n_{i})_{i=1}^{K}.

That is, J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} is consistent and asymptotically normal, with the optimal asymptotic variance n​Var​[J^​(πe,𝐰⋆,𝒟)]n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\mathbf{w}^{\star};\mathcal{D})] achievable within the generalized weighted-IPS estimator class ΓwIPS\Gamma_{\mathrm{wIPS}}. The proof of Theorem 4.2 is given in Appendix E.3.

Remark 2 (Estimated logging policies).

When the logging policies are unknown, we plug in estimates fitted on the training folds. Under mild regularity conditions, J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} remains consistent if these estimates are consistent, but its limiting distribution generally differs from that in Theorem 4.2: the score of J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} is not orthogonal to the propensities, so propensity estimation error enters at first order, as for IPS with estimated propensities (Hirano et al., 2003). The limit in Theorem 4.2 still holds if the resulting fold-wise bias is op(n−1/2)o_{p}(n^{-1/2}), for example when q​πe∈span⁡({πi}i∈[K])q\,\pi_{e}\in\mathrm{span}(\{\pi_{i}\}_{i\in[K]}).

4.3 Theoretical Comparison with Other Estimators

We provide a theoretical comparison of the estimators in terms of their asymptotic variance.

Comparison with J^IPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{IPS}}, J^bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{bIPS}} and J^wIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{wIPS}}.

ΓwIPS\Gamma_{\mathrm{wIPS}} contains the naive IPS estimator (J^IPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{IPS}}), the balanced IPS estimator (J^bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{bIPS}}), and the weighted IPS estimator (J^wIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{wIPS}}). Setting the weights in (3.1) to

wiIPS=nin​r,wibIPS=nin​πiπavg​r,wiwIPS=ni​γ^i​r\displaystyle w_{i}^{\mathrm{IPS}}=\frac{n_{i}}{n}r,\qquad w_{i}^{\mathrm{bIPS}}=\frac{n_{i}}{n}\frac{\pi_{i}}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}}r,\qquad w_{i}^{\mathrm{wIPS}}=n_{i}\hat{\gamma}_{i}r

recovers (2.1), (2.2), and (2.3), respectively. Each choice satisfies the normalization constraint because ∑ini/n=1\sum_{i}n_{i}/n=1, ∑i(ni/n)​πi/πavg=1\sum_{i}(n_{i}/n)\pi_{i}/\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}=1, and ∑ini​γ^i=1\sum_{i}n_{i}\hat{\gamma}_{i}=1. The same identities hold for the cross-fitted version of J^wIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{wIPS}}, conditionally on the training folds, with the held-out stratum sizes in place of nin_{i}. Hence, with known propensities, our asymptotic efficiency result in Theorem 4.2 implies that, for every problem instance,

AVar⁡[J^oIPS​(πe,𝒟)]≤AVar⁡[J^x​(πe,𝒟)],∀x∈{IPS,bIPS,wIPS}\displaystyle\mathrm{AVar}\big[\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})\big]\leq\mathrm{AVar}\big[\hat{J}_{\mathrm{x}}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})\big],\quad\forall\mathrm{x}\in\big\{\mathrm{IPS},\mathrm{bIPS},\mathrm{wIPS}\big\}

where AVar⁡[J^]\mathrm{AVar}[\hat{J}] denotes the variance of the limiting distribution of n′​(J^−J​(πe))\sqrt{n^{\prime}}\,(\hat{J}-J(\pi_{e})). This resolves the dilemma between balanced and weighted IPS noted by Agarwal et al. (2017): asymptotically, J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} is at least as efficient as both.

Comparison with J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}}}.

Rewriting our infeasible optimal estimator J^​(πe,𝜶⋆,𝒟)\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\bm{\alpha}^{\star};\mathcal{D}) (3.4), we have

J^​(πe,𝜶⋆,𝒟)=1n​∑i=1K∑(S,A,R)∈𝒟i[πe​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S)​(R−g𝜶⋆πe​(S,A))+g𝜶⋆πe​(S,πe)],\displaystyle\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\bm{\alpha}^{\star};\mathcal{D})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\sum_{(S,A,R)\in\mathcal{D}_{i}}\left[\frac{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}\left(R-\frac{g_{\bm{\alpha}^{\star}}}{\pi_{e}}(S,A)\right)+\frac{g_{\bm{\alpha}^{\star}}}{\pi_{e}}(S,\pi_{e})\right], (4.2)

where g𝜶⋆≔∑i∈[K]αi⋆​πig_{\bm{\alpha}^{\star}}\coloneq\sum_{i\in[K]}\alpha^{\star}_{i}\pi_{i} and g𝜶⋆πe​(s,πe)≔∫𝒜g𝜶⋆​(s,a)πe​(a∣s)​πe​(a|s)​d​μa​(a)=∑i∈[K]αi⋆\frac{g_{\bm{\alpha}^{\star}}}{\pi_{e}}(s,\pi_{e})\coloneq\int_{\mathcal{A}}\frac{g_{\bm{\alpha}^{\star}}(s,a)}{\pi_{e}(a\mid s)}\pi_{e}(a|s)\,d\mu_{a}(a)=\sum_{i\in[K]}\alpha_{i}^{\star}.

Thus, our estimator belongs to the class of estimators studied by Kallus et al. (2021):

J^Γ​(πe,h,f,𝒟)=1n​∑i=1K∑(S,A,R)∈𝒟i[h⁡(i,S,A)​πe​(A∣S)​(R−f⁡(S,A))+f⁡(S,πe)],\displaystyle\hat{J}_{\Gamma}(\pi_{e},h,f;\mathcal{D})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\sum_{(S,A,R)\in\mathcal{D}_{i}}\big[h(i,S,A)\,\pi_{e}(A\mid S)\big(R-f(S,A)\big)+f(S,\pi_{e})\big],

where hh satisfies ∑i(ni/n)​πi​(a∣s)​h​(i,s,a)=1\sum_{i}(n_{i}/n)\,\pi_{i}(a\mid s)\,h(i,s,a)=1, which makes J^Γ\hat{J}_{\Gamma} unbiased. The optimal variance is achieved by h⁡(i,s,a)=1/πavg​(a∣s)h(i,s,a)=1/\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(a\mid s) for all i∈[K]i\in[K] and f⁡(s,a)=q⁡(s,a)f(s,a)=q(s,a), with q⁡(s,a)q(s,a) denoting the conditional mean reward. This holds even though our weights wiw_{i} may depend on (s,a,r)(s,a,r) while hh depends only on (i,s,a)(i,s,a): the representation (4.2) corresponds to h=1/πavgh=1/\pi_{\mathrm{avg}} and f=g𝜶⋆/πef=g_{\bm{\alpha}^{\star}}/\pi_{e}.

The variance gap between our infeasible estimator J^​(πe,𝐰⋆,𝒟)\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\mathbf{w}^{\star};\mathcal{D}), which is optimal within ΓwIPS\Gamma_{\mathrm{wIPS}}, and the infeasible optimal estimator J^Γ⋆​(πe,𝒟)≔J^Γ​(πe,1/πavg,q,𝒟)\hat{J}^{\star}_{\Gamma}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})\coloneq\hat{J}_{\Gamma}(\pi_{e},1/\pi_{\mathrm{avg}},q;\mathcal{D}) in this class is characterized in terms of the residual from the orthogonal projection of q​πeq\,\pi_{e} onto the finite-dimensional space spanned by the logging policies, span⁡({πi}i∈[K])\mathrm{span}\big(\{\pi_{i}\}_{i\in[K]}\big). The precise statement is given below, with the proof deferred to Appendix E.4.

Theorem 4.3.

The variance gap between J^​(πe,𝛂⋆,𝒟)\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\bm{\alpha}^{\star};\mathcal{D}) and the semiparametrically efficient oracle estimator J^Γ⋆​(πe,𝒟)≔J^Γ​(πe,1/πavg,q,𝒟)\hat{J}^{\star}_{\Gamma}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})\coloneq\hat{J}_{\Gamma}(\pi_{e},1/\pi_{\mathrm{avg}},q;\mathcal{D}) is given by

Var⁡[J^​(πe,𝜶⋆,𝒟)]−Var⁡[J^Γ⋆​(πe,𝒟)]=1n​(inf𝜶∈ℝK‖q​πe−g𝜶‖μlog2−Varps​[q⁡(S,πe)])≥0,\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}\big[\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\bm{\alpha}^{\star};\mathcal{D})\big]-\mathrm{Var}\big[\hat{J}^{\star}_{\Gamma}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})\big]=\frac{1}{n}\left(\inf_{\bm{\alpha}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}}\big\|q\,\pi_{e}-g_{\bm{\alpha}}\big\|^{2}_{\mu_{\log}}-\mathrm{Var}_{p_{s}}\big[q(S,\pi_{e})\big]\right)\geq 0,

where ∥⋅∥μlog\|\cdot\|_{\mu_{\log}} is the norm induced by the inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩μlog\left\langle\cdot,\cdot\right\rangle_{\mu_{\log}}, with d​μlog≔ps/πavg​d​μs,ad\mu_{\log}\coloneq p_{s}/\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}\,d\mu_{s,a}. Moreover, equality holds whenever q​πe∈span⁡({πi}i∈[K])q\,\pi_{e}\in\mathrm{span}\big(\{\pi_{i}\}_{i\in[K]}\big).

Kallus et al. (2021) showed that, for any consistent estimator q^\hat{q} of the conditional mean reward qq, under their regularity conditions, J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}} (2.4) achieves the optimal asymptotic variance n​Var​[J^Γ⋆​(πe,𝒟)]n\mathrm{Var}\big[\hat{J}^{\star}_{\Gamma}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})\big].

Combining this result with Theorem 4.2, we obtain

AVar⁡[J^DR​-​bIPS​(πe,𝒟)]≤AVar⁡[J^oIPS​(πe,𝒟)].\displaystyle\mathrm{AVar}\big[\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})\big]\leq\mathrm{AVar}\big[\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})\big].

We close this gap in Appendix B with a doubly robust extension that uses the same reward model: it applies the control-variate form (3.4) to the residual R−q^​(S,A)R-\hat{q}(S,A) and adds the direct-method term q^​(S,πe)\hat{q}(S,\pi_{e}). We show that, with known logging policies, J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} has asymptotic variance no larger than that of J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}}. Moreover, suppose that both estimators use the same misspecified reward model, q^→q′≠q\hat{q}\to q^{\prime}\neq q. If (q−q′)​πe∈span​{πi}i=1K(q-q^{\prime})\pi_{e}\in\mathrm{span}\{\pi_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K}, then J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} still attains the oracle asymptotic variance n​Var​[J^Γ⋆​(πe,𝒟)]n\mathrm{Var}\big[\hat{J}_{\Gamma}^{\star}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})\big], whereas J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}} in general does not. The reason is that J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} projects (q−q′)​πe(q-q^{\prime})\pi_{e} onto span​{πi}i=1K\mathrm{span}\{\pi_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K} in L2​(μlog)L^{2}(\mu_{\log}) and effectively uses the corrected reward model q′+gΔ/πeq^{\prime}+g^{\Delta}/\pi_{e}, where gΔg^{\Delta} denotes this projection; only the component of (q−q′)​πe(q-q^{\prime})\pi_{e} orthogonal to the span contributes excess variance.

5 Numerical Experiments

5.1 Benchmark Datasets and Experiment Setup

Following prior multi-logger OPE protocols (Agarwal et al., 2017; Kallus et al., 2021), we evaluate on four UCI datasets (Table 1): OptDigits (Alpaydin and Kaynak, 1998), SatImage (Srinivasan, 1993), PenDigits (Alpaydin and Alimoglu, 1996), and Letter (Slate, 1991). Each classification dataset is converted into a contextual bandit dataset by treating labels as actions and assigning reward 11 for a correct action and 00 otherwise.

Mapping Classification Problems to Contextual Bandits.

In deterministic-label multi-class classification, samples take the form (S,y⁡(S))(S,y(S)), where S∼psS\sim p_{s} and y⁡(⋅)y(\cdot) is the ground-truth labeling function. We view this as a contextual bandit problem by treating the feature distribution psp_{s} as the context distribution and defining the deterministic reward as r(s,a)≔𝟙[y(s)=a]r(s,a)\coloneq\mathds{1}[y(s)=a].

To construct the evaluation policy, we train a multinomial logistic classifier on 30% of each dataset and define the deterministic policy πdet(a∣s)≔𝟙[a=y^(s)]\pi_{\mathrm{det}}(a\mid s)\coloneq\mathds{1}[a=\hat{y}(s)]. We set the evaluation policy to πe=πdet\pi_{e}=\pi_{\mathrm{det}}. Because πe\pi_{e} is deterministic, the weights (3.2) are undefined where πe​(a∣s)=0\pi_{e}(a\mid s)=0, so we compute J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} through the control-variate form (3.4), which does not divide by πe\pi_{e} (Remark 1). The remaining 70% of the data is used as an evaluation pool. On this pool, the empirical accuracy of πdet\pi_{\mathrm{det}} is treated as the ground-truth policy value J⁡(πe)J(\pi_{e}).

We generate logged bandit data from the evaluation pool using two logging policies,

π1=0.95⋅πdet+0.05⋅πu,π2=0.05⋅πdet+0.95⋅πu,\displaystyle\pi_{1}=0.95\cdot\pi_{\mathrm{det}}+0.05\cdot\pi_{u},\qquad\pi_{2}=0.05\cdot\pi_{\mathrm{det}}+0.95\cdot\pi_{u},

where πu\pi_{u} is the policy that chooses an action uniformly at random for any context. Thus, π1\pi_{1} is well aligned with πe\pi_{e}, whereas π2\pi_{2} is much less aligned with πe\pi_{e}. For each context in the evaluation pool, we assign it to either 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1} or 𝒟2\mathcal{D}_{2}, sample an action from the corresponding logging policy, and observe the deterministic reward r⁡(s,a)r(s,a). We vary the stratum-size ratio over n1/n2∈{0.1,0.25,0.5,1,2,4,10}n_{1}/n_{2}\in\{0.1,0.25,0.5,1,2,4,10\}. Smaller ratios make the logged dataset more dominated by π2\pi_{2}. Here the two loggers explore uniformly with probabilities 0.050.05 and 0.950.95 (the weights on πu\pi_{u} above). Appendix D uses (0.20,0.80)(0.20,0.80) and (0.35,0.65)(0.35,0.65), and Appendix C uses (0.05,0.50,0.95)(0.05,0.50,0.95) for K=3K=3 and (0.05,0.15,0.30,0.70,0.95)(0.05,0.15,0.30,0.70,0.95) for K=5K=5.

We benchmark each estimator J^\hat{J} against the ground-truth value J⁡(πe)J(\pi_{e}) using relative root mean squared error. For MM independent trials with ground-truth values JmJ_{m} and J¯=M−1​∑mJm\bar{J}=M^{-1}\sum_{m}J_{m}, this metric is

Relative-RMSE​(J^)≔1J¯​1M​∑m=1M(Jm−J^m)2,\displaystyle\textup{Relative-RMSE}(\hat{J})\coloneq\frac{1}{\bar{J}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\left(J_{m}-\hat{J}_{m}\right)^{2}}, (5.1)

where J^m\hat{J}_{m} denotes the estimated policy value in the mm-th trial. To separate bias from variance, we also report the squared bias (M−1​∑m=1M(J^m−Jm))2\big(M^{-1}\sum_{m=1}^{M}(\hat{J}_{m}-J_{m})\big)^{2} and the empirical standard deviation of J^1,…,J^M\hat{J}_{1},\dots,\hat{J}_{M} (Appendix A). We use M=200M=200 trials and report 95%95\% paired percentile-bootstrap intervals. Each of the B=2,000B=2{,}000 bootstrap resamples draws MM trial indices with replacement and recomputes Relative-RMSE for every estimator from the same indices and the matching ground-truth values JmJ_{m}; the interval endpoints are the 2.52.5th and 97.597.5th percentiles. Because each trial redraws the data split, the logged actions, and the cross-fitting folds, the intervals reflect all three sources of variation. To compare two estimators, we apply the same procedure to the difference of their Relative-RMSEs computed on the same resampled trials.

Estimators Considered.

We compare J^IPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{IPS}} (Eq. 2.1), J^bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{bIPS}} (Eq. 2.2), J^wIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{wIPS}} (Eq. 2.3), our J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} (§3), J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}} (Kallus et al., 2021), and our J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} (Appendix B). The two DR estimators use the same reward model q^\hat{q}, a logistic regression fitted with two-fold cross-fitting, and the same folds: for both, every reward, propensity, and weight quantity is fitted on the training fold and evaluated on the same held-out observations. In all experiments, we compute 𝜶^(z)\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)} with NumPy’s Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse (numpy.linalg.pinv, default relative cutoff 10−1510^{-15}). In the designs with K≥3K\geq 3 loggers (Appendices C and F), every logger is a mixture of the same two policies, so 𝐓\mathbf{T} has rank two and the pseudoinverse returns the minimum-norm least-squares solution whenever 𝐓^(z)\hat{\mathbf{T}}^{(z)} is singular. Appendix A details estimation of unknown logging policies.

The experimental results are reported and discussed in Appendix A. In summary, J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} generally improves over existing multi-logger IPS baselines across benchmark datasets and logger mixtures, and the DR extension J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}}} achieves lower Relative-RMSE than J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}}} in many finite-sample settings. In a synthetic experiment with n=106n=10^{6} samples (Appendix F.3), J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} attains a Relative-RMSE of 1.99×10−41.99\times 10^{-4}, compared with 5.44×10−45.44\times 10^{-4} for J^wIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{wIPS}}. Code to reproduce the experiments is included in the supplementary material and will be publicly released.

6 Conclusion

We studied off-policy evaluation with multiple logging policies, where existing IPS estimators can have highly instance-dependent performance. We addressed this by deriving J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}, an asymptotically variance-minimizing estimator within the generalized weighted-IPS class ΓwIPS\Gamma_{\mathrm{wIPS}}, which contains previously considered IPS estimators. The optimal weights have a closed-form characterization through the linear system 𝐓​𝜶=𝐜\mathbf{T}\bm{\alpha}=\mathbf{c}, whose entries can be estimated from logged data, leading to a practical cross-fitted estimator. This gives a principled way to choose sample-dependent IPS weights rather than selecting among fixed rules such as naive IPS, balanced IPS, and weighted IPS.

We also related J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} to the semiparametric efficiency framework of Kallus et al. (2021). The linear system 𝐓​𝜶=𝐜\mathbf{T}\bm{\alpha}=\mathbf{c} has a projection interpretation: it chooses the best control variate representable by the logging policies. When this space is rich enough, J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} asymptotically recovers the efficient oracle. Otherwise, the projection residual characterizes the variance gap. We further extended the estimator to a doubly robust version, J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}}, which matches the asymptotic variance of the efficient DR baseline when the reward model is correctly specified and can be more robust under certain structured misspecifications.

Empirically, J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} improves over existing multi-logger IPS baselines across benchmark datasets and logger mixtures, and J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} often improves over the DR balanced IPS baseline in finite samples. The main limitation is that our optimality result is restricted to ΓwIPS\Gamma_{\mathrm{wIPS}} and our asymptotic guarantees assume known logging policies; with estimated propensities, the limiting variance generally changes (Remark 2). We also do not analyze finite-sample behavior or the stability of the estimated weights, the method relies on sufficient overlap, and our experiments cover UCI benchmarks and one synthetic environment. Future work includes finite-sample analysis, richer basis classes beyond logging policies, and extensions to sequential settings.

Appendix A Main Experimental Results and Discussion

This appendix reports the full experimental results for the setup described in §5. Figures 1 and 2 show Relative-RMSE on Letter, OptDigits, PenDigits, and SatImage across the stratum-size ratios n1/n2∈{0.1,0.25,0.5,1,2,4,10}n_{1}/n_{2}\in\{0.1,0.25,0.5,1,2,4,10\}. Each point is computed from M=200M=200 independent trials, and our estimator J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} uses Z=5Z=5 folds.

When Logging Policies are Unknown.

For non-DR estimators with unknown logging policies, we estimate each logging policy π^i\hat{\pi}_{i} separately using 2-fold cross-fitted multinomial logistic regression within each logger. The out-of-fold models are used to estimate the observed-action propensities π^i​(Ai​j∣Si​j)\hat{\pi}_{i}(A_{ij}\mid S_{ij}) for samples in stratum ii. We also fit a model on all samples from stratum ii and use it to evaluate π^i​(Ak​j∣Sk​j)\hat{\pi}_{i}(A_{kj}\mid S_{kj}) for samples from all strata, which is needed when an estimator requires the propensity of a sample under a different logging policy.

For numerical stability, we blend each predicted action distribution with a 1% uniform distribution and clip all propensities below 10−310^{-3}. For degenerate strata, such as strata with too few samples or only one observed action class, we instead use the uniform policy. The resulting estimated logging policies are then plugged into IPS-style estimators.

Known Logging Policies.

When logging policies are known (Figure 1), J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} consistently improves over non-DR IPS baselines across datasets and stratum-size ratios. In several regimes, it is also competitive with or better than J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}}. Adding a reward model (J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}}) improves only slightly on J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}, which suggests that little residual structure remains after the control-variate correction. These results support the practical value of the control-variate form (3.4), which uses the logger-basis structure to reduce variance without requiring a conditional reward estimator. By contrast, J^IPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{IPS}} and J^bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{bIPS}} often show larger errors, especially at small n1/n2n_{1}/n_{2}, where the logged data are dominated by the less aligned logger π2\pi_{2}.

Estimated Logging Policies.

When logging policies are estimated (Figure 2), the same qualitative trend persists: J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} remains strong and generally outperforms non-DR baselines (J^IPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{IPS}}, J^bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{bIPS}}, J^wIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{wIPS}}) across datasets and most stratum-size ratios. This is consistent with sample-dependent, cross-fitted weighting through 𝐓^\hat{\mathbf{T}} and 𝐜^\hat{\mathbf{c}}, which stabilizes stratum balancing under propensity-estimation noise. In contrast, J^wIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{wIPS}} can underperform J^bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{bIPS}} because its adaptive mixture weights depend on plug-in divergence estimates that are themselves sensitive to estimation noise.

Relative to the DR baseline J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}}}, J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} is not uniformly better when logging policies are estimated; this regime is not covered by Theorem 4.2 (Remark 2). However, the natural DR extension J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}}} achieves lower Relative-RMSE than J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}}} in many settings, particularly at low stratum-size ratios where the data are dominated by the less aligned logger. Subtracting the reward model first shrinks the inverse-propensity-weighted term πe​(R−q^)/πavg\pi_{e}(R-\hat{q})/\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}, and J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} then applies the control-variate correction to this smaller residual, which can improve accuracy in finite samples.

Summary.

Overall, J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} is a strong practical estimator for multi-logger OPE, especially against IPS baselines, and its DR extension J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}}} is often strongest when propensities are estimated. Appendices C and D show that these trends persist with more than two loggers and under alternative mixture settings. Across all settings, J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} has a lower Relative-RMSE than each non-DR baseline in 276276 of 276276 configuration–baseline comparisons with known propensities and in 262262 of 276276 with estimated propensities. J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} has a lower Relative-RMSE than J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}} in 9292 of 9292 and 6666 of 9292 configurations, respectively, and the paired 95%95\% interval for the difference lies below zero in 8989 and 6464 of them.

Table 2 separates the error of each estimator into squared bias and empirical standard deviation at three representative stratum-size ratios. The squared bias is at most 1.5%1.5\% of the variance in every cell, so the differences in Relative-RMSE come mainly from variance, and the smallest standard deviation is attained by J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} or J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} in all twelve dataset–ratio pairs.

Appendix B Doubly Robust Extension of J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}

In this section, we present a doubly robust (DR) extension of our variationally optimal estimator J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}. Given any conditional reward estimator q^:𝒮×𝒜→ℝ\hat{q}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}, we show how to incorporate q^\hat{q} to obtain a DR version of J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}, denoted by J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}}}. We then compare J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}}} both theoretically and empirically with the semiparametrically efficient estimator J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}}}.

B.1 Generalized Weighted DR-IPS Estimator Class ΓDRwIPS\Gamma_{\mathrm{DRwIPS}}

We define the generalized weighted DR-IPS estimator class ΓDRwIPS\Gamma_{\mathrm{DRwIPS}} as follows. Let q^:𝒮×𝒜→ℝ\hat{q}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R} be an estimator of the conditional mean reward q(s,a)≔𝔼[R|S=s,A=a]q(s,a)\coloneq\mathbb{E}[R\,|\,S=s,A=a], and define

J^DM​(πe,q^,𝒟)≔1n​∑i=1K∑(S,A,R)∈𝒟i∫𝒜q^​(S,a)​πe​(a∣S)​d​μa​(a)\displaystyle\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DM}}(\pi_{e},\hat{q};\mathcal{D})\coloneq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\sum_{(S,A,R)\in\mathcal{D}_{i}}\int_{\mathcal{A}}\hat{q}(S,a)\,\pi_{e}(a\mid S)\,d\mu_{a}(a)

as the direct value estimator induced by q^\hat{q}.

Then, the estimator class ΓDRwIPS\Gamma_{\mathrm{DRwIPS}} consists of estimators of the following form:

J^​(πe,𝐰,q^,𝒟)≔J^DM​(πe,q^,𝒟)+∑i=1K1ni​∑(S,A,R)∈𝒟iwi​(S,A,R)⋅πe​(A∣S)πi​(A∣S).\displaystyle\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\mathbf{w},\hat{q};\mathcal{D})\coloneq\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DM}}(\pi_{e},\hat{q};\mathcal{D})+\sum_{i=1}^{K}\frac{1}{n_{i}}\sum_{(S,A,R)\in\mathcal{D}_{i}}w_{i}(S,A,R)\cdot\frac{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{i}(A\mid S)}. (B.1)

where Δ⁡(s,a,r)≔r−q^​(s,a)\Delta(s,a,r)\coloneq r-\hat{q}(s,a) is the residual. The estimator is unbiased when q^\hat{q} is a fixed function, or conditionally on the training data when q^\hat{q} is fitted on data independent of 𝒟\mathcal{D}, provided the weights satisfy the following constraints:

  1. (i)

    Normalization: ∑i=1Kwi​(s,a,r)=Δ⁡(s,a,r)\sum_{i=1}^{K}w_{i}(s,a,r)=\Delta(s,a,r),

  2. (ii)

    Dominance: πi​(a|s)=0⟹wi​(s,a,r)=0\pi_{i}(a|s)=0\implies w_{i}(s,a,r)=0.

Intuitively, this form follows from the decomposition

𝔼μπe​[R]=𝔼μπe​[R−q^]+𝔼μπe​[q^].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{e}}}[R]=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{e}}}[R-\hat{q}]+\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{e}}}[\hat{q}].

That is, we apply weighted IPS to the residual term and use the direct method for the second term.

B.2 Feasible Extension: J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}}

We seek to minimize the variance of (B.1). The variational approach used for J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} applies directly here, with the target variable rr replaced by the residual Δ⁡(s,a,r)≔r−q^​(s,a)\Delta(s,a,r)\coloneq r-\hat{q}(s,a).

Following the same cross-fitting procedure described in §3 for constructing the feasible estimator J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}, we obtain a feasible doubly robust extension, denoted J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}}. For each fold zz, let q^(z)\hat{q}^{(z)} denote the conditional reward estimator trained on 𝒟(−z)\mathcal{D}^{(-z)}. On the held-out fold 𝒟(z)\mathcal{D}^{(z)}, define the fold-specific direct-method term by

J^DM​(πe,q^(z),𝒟(z))≔1n(z)​∑i=1K∑(S,A,R)∈𝒟i(z)∫𝒜q^(z)​(S,a)​πe​(a∣S)​d​μa​(a).\displaystyle\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DM}}\left(\pi_{e},\hat{q}^{(z)};\mathcal{D}^{(z)}\right)\coloneq\frac{1}{n^{(z)}}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\sum_{(S,A,R)\in\mathcal{D}_{i}^{(z)}}\int_{\mathcal{A}}\hat{q}^{(z)}(S,a)\,\pi_{e}(a\mid S)\,d\mu_{a}(a).

The residual IPS component is obtained by applying the control-variate form (3.4) to the residuals R−q^(z)​(S,A)R-\hat{q}^{(z)}(S,A). Specifically, let

J^Δ​(πe,𝜶^(z),𝒟(z))\displaystyle\hat{J}_{\Delta}\!\left(\pi_{e},\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)};\mathcal{D}^{(z)}\right)
≔1n(z)​∑i∈[K]∑(S,A,R)∈𝒟i(z)[(R−q^(z)​(S,A))​πe​(A∣S)πavg(z)​(A∣S)−∑k∈[K]α^k(z)​πk​(A∣S)πavg(z)​(A∣S)+∑k∈[K]α^k(z)],\displaystyle\hskip-72.26999pt\coloneq\frac{1}{n^{(z)}}\sum_{i\in[K]}\sum_{(S,A,R)\in\mathcal{D}_{i}^{(z)}}\left[\frac{\big(R-\hat{q}^{(z)}(S,A)\big)\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}^{(z)}(A\mid S)}-\frac{\sum_{k\in[K]}\hat{\alpha}^{(z)}_{k}\pi_{k}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}^{(z)}(A\mid S)}+\sum_{k\in[K]}\hat{\alpha}^{(z)}_{k}\right],

where

πavg(z)≔1n(z)​∑i∈[K]ni(z)​πi.\displaystyle\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}^{(z)}\coloneq\frac{1}{n^{(z)}}\sum_{i\in[K]}n_{i}^{(z)}\pi_{i}.

The feasible DR​-​oIPS{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} estimator is then

J^DR​-​oIPS​(πe,𝒟)≔1n​∑z=1Zn(z)​[J^DM​(πe,q^(z),𝒟(z))+J^Δ​(πe,𝜶^(z),𝒟(z))]\displaystyle\boxed{\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})\coloneq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{z=1}^{Z}n^{(z)}\left[\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DM}}\left(\pi_{e},\hat{q}^{(z)};\mathcal{D}^{(z)}\right)+\hat{J}_{\Delta}\!\left(\pi_{e},\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)};\mathcal{D}^{(z)}\right)\right]} (B.2)

Shared outer-fold procedure.

Both DR estimators split each stratum into the same two folds (Z=2Z=2). For each fold zz:

  1. 1.

    On the training data 𝒟(−z)\mathcal{D}^{(-z)}, fit the reward model q^(z)\hat{q}^{(z)}, the logging-policy models when the propensities are unknown, and the moments 𝐓^(z)\hat{\mathbf{T}}^{(z)} and 𝐜^(z)\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{(z)} defined below, and set 𝜶^(z)=(𝐓^(z))†​𝐜^(z)\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)}=(\hat{\mathbf{T}}^{(z)})^{\dagger}\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{(z)}.

  2. 2.

    Evaluate both estimators on the held-out data 𝒟(z)\mathcal{D}^{(z)}, using 𝜶^(z)\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)} for J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} and 𝜶^(z)=0\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)}=0 for J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}}.

The fold estimates are combined as in (B.2). With 𝜶^(z)=0\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)}=0, this yields the cross-fitted form of (2.4) with q^(z)\hat{q}^{(z)} and πavg(z)\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}^{(z)}.

Estimation of Coefficients.

As in J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}, the parameters 𝜶^(z)\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)} in (B.2) are obtained from 𝐓​𝜶=𝐜\mathbf{T}\bm{\alpha}=\mathbf{c} via cross-fitting. Specifically, 𝜶^(z)=(𝐓^(z))†​𝐜^(z)\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)}=(\hat{\mathbf{T}}^{(z)})^{\dagger}\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{(z)}, where 𝐓^(z)\hat{\mathbf{T}}^{(z)} and 𝐜^(z)\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{(z)} are estimated on 𝒟(−z)\mathcal{D}^{(-z)} as follows.

  1. (i)

    Technique Matrix. 𝐓\mathbf{T} depends only on propensities and sample sizes, so it is identical to the IPS case:

    T^i​j(z)≔1|𝒟i(−z)|​∑(S,A,R)∈𝒟i(−z)πj​(A∣S)πavg(−z)​(A∣S).\displaystyle\hat{T}_{ij}^{(z)}\coloneq\frac{1}{\big|\mathcal{D}^{(-z)}_{i}\big|}\sum_{(S,A,R)\in\mathcal{D}^{(-z)}_{i}}\frac{\pi_{j}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}^{(-z)}(A\mid S)}.
  2. (ii)

    Contribution Vector. The vector 𝐜\mathbf{c} depends on the target signal. For DR, we use residuals R−q^(z)​(S,A)R-\hat{q}^{(z)}(S,A) in place of RR:

    c^i(z)≔1|𝒟i(−z)|​∑(S,A,R)∈𝒟i(−z)(R−q^(z)​(S,A))​πe​(A∣S)πavg(−z)​(A∣S).\displaystyle\hat{c}_{i}^{(z)}\coloneq\frac{1}{\big|\mathcal{D}^{(-z)}_{i}\big|}\sum_{(S,A,R)\in\mathcal{D}^{(-z)}_{i}}\frac{\,\big(R-\hat{q}^{(z)}(S,A)\big)\,\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}^{(-z)}(A\mid S)}.

Here, πavg(−z)≔1n(−z)​∑i∈[K]ni(−z)​πi\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}^{(-z)}\coloneq\frac{1}{n^{(-z)}}\sum_{i\in[K]}n_{i}^{(-z)}\pi_{i}, with n(−z)≔∑i∈[K]ni(−z)n^{(-z)}\coloneq\sum_{i\in[K]}n_{i}^{(-z)}, as in the main text, §3.2. When the logging policies are unknown, we replace the propensities in the above expressions by their cross-fitted estimates.

B.3 Theoretical Comparison with the Optimal Estimator of Kallus et al. [2021]

In this section, we provide a theoretical comparison between J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} and J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}}. The purpose is to explain how the residual version of our variational construction relates to the semiparametrically efficient estimator studied in Kallus et al. [2021].

The comparison has two implications.

  1. (i)

    When q^\hat{q} is a consistent estimator of the conditional mean reward q⁡(s,a)q(s,a), both J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} and J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}} attain the same semiparametrically efficient oracle variance asymptotically.

  2. (ii)

    When q^\hat{q} is misspecified, J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} can remain variance-optimal in cases where the misspecification lies in the logger-basis space, whereas J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}} need not.

With known logging policies and under the conditions of Theorem 4.2, these conclusions follow from the following lemma, proved in Appendix E.

Let q(s,a)≔𝔼[R|S=s,A=a]q(s,a)\coloneq\mathbb{E}[R\,|\,S=s,A=a] denote the conditional mean reward, and define mi​(f)≔𝔼μπi​[(q−f)​πe/πavg]−𝔼ps​[(q−f)​(S,πe)]m_{i}(f)\coloneq\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{i}}}[(q-f)\pi_{e}/\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}]-\mathbb{E}_{p_{s}}[(q-f)(S,\pi_{e})]. Consistent reward estimation.

We first explain how J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} fits into the J^Γ\hat{J}_{\Gamma} class. For fixed q^\hat{q} and 𝜶\bm{\alpha}, the infeasible version of J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} has summand

q^​(S,πe)+πe​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S)​(R−q^​(S,A))−g𝜶​(S,A)πavg​(A∣S)+∑i∈[K]αi.\displaystyle\hat{q}(S,\pi_{e})+\frac{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}\big(R-\hat{q}(S,A)\big)-\frac{g_{\bm{\alpha}}(S,A)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}+\sum_{i\in[K]}\alpha_{i}.

J^Γ​(πe,q^+g𝜶πe,𝒟).\displaystyle\hat{J}_{\Gamma}\!\left(\pi_{e},\hat{q}+\frac{g_{\bm{\alpha}}}{\pi_{e}};\mathcal{D}\right).

The role of 𝜶\bm{\alpha} is to choose g𝜶g_{\bm{\alpha}} as the projection of (q−q^)​πe(q-\hat{q})\pi_{e} onto span⁡({πi}i∈[K])\mathrm{span}\big(\{\pi_{i}\}_{i\in[K]}\big). In other words, J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} corrects q^\hat{q} only in directions that can be represented by the logging policies.

If q^\hat{q} is consistent for qq, then (q−q^)​πe(q-\hat{q})\pi_{e} converges to zero, so its projection g𝜶g_{\bm{\alpha}} also converges to zero. Therefore,

q^+g𝜶πe→q.\displaystyle\hat{q}+\frac{g_{\bm{\alpha}}}{\pi_{e}}\to q.

Applying Lemma B.3 to the limiting regression function f=qf=q shows that the asymptotic excess variance of J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} over the oracle estimator J^Γ⋆​(πe,𝒟)≔J^Γ​(πe,q,𝒟)\hat{J}^{\star}_{\Gamma}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})\coloneq\hat{J}_{\Gamma}(\pi_{e},q;\mathcal{D}) vanishes. By Kallus et al. [2021], the same is true for J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}} when q^\hat{q} is consistent for qq. Hence, in the well-specified case, J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} and J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}} have the same asymptotic variance, namely n​Var​[J^Γ⋆​(πe,𝒟)]n\mathrm{Var}\big[\hat{J}^{\star}_{\Gamma}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})\big].

Now suppose that q^\hat{q} converges to a misspecified limit q′q^{\prime}. Then J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}} corresponds asymptotically to

J^Γ​(πe,q′,𝒟),\displaystyle\hat{J}_{\Gamma}(\pi_{e},q^{\prime};\mathcal{D}),

so Lemma B.3 characterizes its asymptotic excess variance over the oracle by taking f=q′f=q^{\prime}.

J^Γ​(πe,q′+g𝜶⋆πe,𝒟),\displaystyle\hat{J}_{\Gamma}\!\left(\pi_{e},q^{\prime}+\frac{g_{\bm{\alpha}^{\star}}}{\pi_{e}};\mathcal{D}\right),

In particular, if

(q−q′)​πe∈span⁡({πi}i∈[K]),\displaystyle(q-q^{\prime})\pi_{e}\in\mathrm{span}\big(\{\pi_{i}\}_{i\in[K]}\big),

then g𝜶⋆=(q−q′)​πeg_{\bm{\alpha}^{\star}}=(q-q^{\prime})\pi_{e}, and hence

Thus, J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} attains the oracle asymptotic variance even though q^\hat{q} is misspecified. In contrast, J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}} remains tied to q′q^{\prime} and may have nonzero asymptotic excess variance. This is the sense in which J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} is more robust to misspecification in directions spanned by the logging policies.

B.4 Empirical Comparison with the Optimal Estimator of Kallus et al. [2021]

We provide an alternative, side-by-side presentation of the experimental results from §5, in Figure 3 to more directly compare J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} with J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}}, which is known to be asymptotically optimal within the class studied by Kallus et al. [2021]. We also summarize the nuisance estimation procedures used in these experiments.

Nuisance Estimation.

We summarize how nuisance components (logging policies and conditional rewards) are estimated.

  • •

    Logging policies (π^i\hat{\pi}_{i}): We estimate logging policies with multinomial logistic regression and 2-fold cross-fitting. To maintain numerical stability in both the technique-matrix estimate 𝐓^\hat{\mathbf{T}} and the denominator of Eq. (B.2), we clip the estimated propensities to the range [10−3,1][10^{-3},1] after 1%1\% uniform smoothing.

  • •

    Conditional rewards (q^\hat{q}): We estimate q(s,a)≔𝔼[r|s,a]q(s,a)\coloneq\mathbb{E}[r|s,a] via logistic regression with 2-fold cross-fitting, using the same protocol as for logging policies. Actions are represented with one-hot encodings.

Findings.

In the setting of Figure 3, J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}} has a lower Relative-RMSE than J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}} in 1616 of 2828 configurations. Across all 184184 configurations (9292 with known and 9292 with estimated propensities), it has a lower Relative-RMSE in 158158, and the paired 95%95\% interval for the difference lies below zero in 153153.

Appendix C Empirical Results with K>2K>2 Logging Policies

We extend the two-logger experiment to heterogeneous mixtures with K∈{3,5}K\in\{3,5\} logging policies. As before, we train a multinomial logistic regression model on a training split to obtain a deterministic base policy πdet\pi_{\mathrm{det}} and set the evaluation policy to πe=πdet\pi_{e}=\pi_{\mathrm{det}}. The reward is deterministic: r(s,a)≔𝟙[y(s)=a]r(s,a)\coloneq\mathds{1}\left[y(s)=a\right], where y⁡(s)y(s) is the label of context s∈ℝds\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. The ground-truth policy value is therefore the classification accuracy of πe\pi_{e} on the OPE sample.

J(πe)=𝔼A∼πe(⋅∣S),S∼ps[𝟙[y(S)=A]].\displaystyle J(\pi_{e})=\mathbb{E}_{A\sim\pi_{e}(\cdot\mid S),S\sim p_{s}}\big[\mathds{1}\left[y(S)=A\right]\big].

We construct K∈{3,5}K\in\{3,5\} logging policies by mixing πdet\pi_{\mathrm{det}} with the uniform policy πu\pi_{u} (which ignores context and selects actions uniformly). For K=5K=5, let βi∈{0.05,0.15,0.30,0.70,0.95}\beta_{i}\in\{0.05,0.15,0.30,0.70,0.95\} and define, for i=1,…,Ki=1,\dots,K,

πi​(a|s)≔(1−βi)⋅πdet​(a|s)+βi|𝒜|.\displaystyle\pi_{i}(a|s)\coloneq(1-\beta_{i})\cdot\pi_{\mathrm{det}}(a|s)+\frac{\beta_{i}}{|\mathcal{A}|}.

The OPE sample is generated from an equal-weight logger mixture, with stratum weights τi=0.2\tau_{i}=0.2 for K=5K=5 and τi=13\tau_{i}=\tfrac{1}{3} for K=3K=3 (so ni/n≈τin_{i}/n\approx\tau_{i}, up to integer rounding). We partition the OPE sample into these strata, sample a∼πi(⋅∣s)a\sim\pi_{i}(\cdot\mid s) in stratum ii, and assign reward r(s,a)≔𝟙[y(s)=a]r(s,a)\coloneq\mathds{1}[y(s)=a]. For K=3K=3, we use βi∈{0.05,0.5,0.95}\beta_{i}\in\{0.05,0.5,0.95\}.

Results.

Across settings with up to five loggers (Figure 4 and Figure 5), our logger-basis IPS estimator J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} generally achieves strong accuracy when the logging policies are known, while its doubly robust extension J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}}} tends to perform best when the logging policies are estimated.

When logging policies are estimated, J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}}} outperforms J^DR​-​bIPS\hat{J}_{{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{bIPS}}} on all four datasets for K=5K=5 and three of four for K=3K=3. Among the non-DR estimators, J^IPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{IPS}} and J^wIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{wIPS}} can become unstable (particularly on OptDigits). This instability appears when estimated logging propensities are near zero or noisy in specific strata, yielding extreme 1/π^i​(a|s)1/\hat{\pi}_{i}(a|s) weights and heavy-tailed variance. By comparison, the sample-dependent weighting in J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} and J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}}} better controls variance and produces substantially more stable estimates. The same qualitative pattern holds for three loggers (Figures 6 and 7).

Appendix D Sensitivity to the Additive Mixture of Logging Policies

We repeat the main experiments with alternative mixture ratios between the deterministic policy πdet\pi_{\mathrm{det}} and the uniform policy πu\pi_{u}. For η∈{0.80,0.65}\eta\in\{0.80,0.65\}, define

π1(η)=η​πdet+(1−η)​πu,π2(η)=(1−η)​πdet+η​πu.\displaystyle\pi^{(\eta)}_{1}\;=\;\eta\,\pi_{\mathrm{det}}+(1-\eta)\,\pi_{u},\quad\pi^{(\eta)}_{2}\;=\;(1-\eta)\,\pi_{\mathrm{det}}+\eta\,\pi_{u}.

All other settings, including the evaluation policy πe=πdet\pi_{e}=\pi_{\mathrm{det}}, datasets, train/evaluation split ratio, stratum-size ratios n1/n2n_{1}/n_{2}, number of repeats M=200M=200, and non-DR cross-fitting folds Z=5Z=5, match the main-text protocol. Both DR estimators use the shared two-fold procedure of Appendix B.

Results.

Across both additive mixtures (η=0.80\eta=0.80 and η=0.65\eta=0.65), the qualitative trends in Figures 8, 9, 10, and 11 remain consistent with the main-text results. Our logger-basis IPS estimator and its DR extension (J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} and J^DR​-​oIPS\hat{J}_{{\mathrm{DR}\text{-}\mathrm{oIPS}}}) remain among the strongest methods in known- and estimated-logging settings, respectively. Improvements are most pronounced in low-overlap regimes (small n1/n2n_{1}/n_{2}), while gaps narrow as overlap increases. Estimated propensities increase absolute errors and can change which estimator ranks first.

Proof of Theorem 4.1.

Since the objective in (4.1) is the variance of a linear functional of 𝐰\mathbf{w}, the variance minimization problem subject to the normalization constraint is convex. We therefore derive the first-order stationarity condition for the Lagrange-augmented functional I⁡[𝐰,λ]I[\mathbf{w},\lambda] defined below.

Recall ρr​(ω)=r\rho_{r}(\omega)=r for ω=(s,a,r)\omega=(s,a,r). Define the functional I⁡[𝐰,λ]I[\mathbf{w},\lambda] as

=Var⁡[J^​(πe,𝐰,𝒟)]−∑i=1K⟨λ,wi⟩μπe+⟨λ,ρr⟩μπe,\displaystyle=\mathrm{Var}\big[\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\mathbf{w};\mathcal{D})\big]-\sum_{i=1}^{K}\left\langle\lambda,w_{i}\right\rangle_{\mu_{\pi_{e}}}+\left\langle\lambda,\rho_{r}\right\rangle_{\mu_{\pi_{e}}},

where λ:Ω→ℝ\lambda:\Omega\to\mathbb{R} is the Lagrange multiplier enforcing the normalization constraint.

Next, for a perturbation direction 𝜹⁡(ω)≔(δi​(ω))i∈[K]\bm{\delta}(\omega)\coloneq(\delta_{i}(\omega))_{i\in[K]} and ϵ∈ℝK\bm{\epsilon}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}, define I⁡(ϵ,𝜹,𝐰,λ)I(\bm{\epsilon};\bm{\delta},\mathbf{w},\lambda) as

I⁡(ϵ,𝜹,𝐰,λ)≔I⁡[w1+ϵ1​δ1,…,wK+ϵK​δK,λ],\displaystyle I(\bm{\epsilon};\bm{\delta},\mathbf{w},\lambda)\coloneq I[w_{1}+\epsilon_{1}\delta_{1},\dots,w_{K}+\epsilon_{K}\delta_{K},\lambda],

which can be interpreted as the variation of I⁡[𝐰,λ]I[\mathbf{w},\lambda] under perturbations along the direction 𝜹\bm{\delta}.

To verify optimality, it suffices to exhibit feasible 𝐰⋆\mathbf{w}^{\star} and λ⋆\lambda^{\star} such that, for every perturbation 𝜹\bm{\delta} with finite weighted second moments and each i∈[K]i\in[K],

⟨δi,2​wi⋆​πeni​πi−2​⟨wi⋆,1⟩μπeni−λ⋆⟩μπe=0.\displaystyle\left\langle\delta_{i},\frac{2w^{\star}_{i}\pi_{e}}{n_{i}\pi_{i}}-\frac{2\left\langle w^{\star}_{i},1\right\rangle_{\mu_{\pi_{e}}}}{n_{i}}-\lambda^{\star}\right\rangle_{\mu_{\pi_{e}}}=0. (E.1)
