−nin∑j=1Kαj𝔼μπe[πi​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S)πj​(A∣S)πe​(A∣S)].\displaystyle\qquad\qquad-\frac{n_{i}}{n}\,\sum^{K}_{j=1}\alpha_{j}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{e}}}\!\left[\frac{\pi_{i}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}\,\frac{\pi_{j}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}\right]. (E.4)

Since

𝔼μπe​[πi​(A∣S)πe​(A∣S)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{e}}}\!\left[\frac{\pi_{i}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}\right] =∫Ωπi​(a|s)πe​(a|s)​pr​(r|s,a)​πe​(a|s)​ps​(s)​𝑑μ​(ω)\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\frac{\pi_{i}(a|s)}{\pi_{e}(a|s)}\,p_{r}(r|s,a)\,\pi_{e}(a|s)\,p_{s}(s)\,d\mu(\omega)
=∫Ωpr​(r|s,a)​πi​(a|s)​ps​(s)​𝑑μ​(ω)\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}p_{r}(r|s,a)\,\pi_{i}(a|s)\,p_{s}(s)\,d\mu(\omega)
=∫Ωμπi​(ω)=1,\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\mu_{\pi_{i}}(\omega)=1,

and

Ti​j\displaystyle T_{ij} ≔𝔼μπi​[πj​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S)]=𝔼μπe​[πi​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S)​πj​(A∣S)πe​(A∣S)]\displaystyle\coloneq\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{i}}}\!\left[\frac{\pi_{j}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{e}}}\!\left[\frac{\pi_{i}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}\,\frac{\pi_{j}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}\right]
ci\displaystyle c_{i} ≔𝔼μπi​[R​πe​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S)]=𝔼μπe​[R​πi​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S)]\displaystyle\coloneq\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{i}}}\!\left[\frac{R\,\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{e}}}\!\left[\frac{R\,\pi_{i}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}\right]

The self-consistency equation (E.4) can be written as 𝐓​𝜶=𝐜\mathbf{T}\bm{\alpha}=\mathbf{c} with 𝐓\mathbf{T} and 𝐜\mathbf{c} given in (3.3).

Finally, by Lemma E.2, 𝐓​𝜶=𝐜\mathbf{T}\bm{\alpha}=\mathbf{c} admits a solution. Hence, the corresponding weights 𝐰\mathbf{w} satisfy the first-order optimality condition (E.1) and therefore solve the variance minimization convex program (4.1). ∎

E.3 Proof of Unbiasedness and Asymptotic Variance Optimality of J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}

In this section, we prove that J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} is unbiased and asymptotically normal, with asymptotic variance n​Var​[J^​(πe,𝐰⋆,𝒟)]n\mathrm{Var}\big[\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\mathbf{w}^{\star};\mathcal{D})\big], which is optimal within ΓwIPS\Gamma_{\mathrm{wIPS}}.

See 4.2

Proof of Theorem 4.2.

We first prove the unbiasedness of J^oIPS​(πe,𝒟)\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D}) when the logging policies are known.

Unbiasedness.

We begin by rewriting the expectation of J^oIPS​(πe,𝒟)\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D}) as an iterated expectation, conditioning on the data 𝒟(−z)\mathcal{D}^{(-z)} used to estimate the nuisance parameter 𝜶\bm{\alpha}:

𝔼⁡[J^oIPS​(πe,𝒟)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})\right] =1n​∑z=1Zn(z)​𝔼​[J^​(πe,𝜶^(z),𝒟(z))]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{z=1}^{Z}n^{(z)}\,\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)};\mathcal{D}^{(z)})\right]
=1n​∑z=1Zn(z)​𝔼​[𝔼⁡[J^​(πe,𝜶^(z),𝒟(z))|𝒟(−z)]]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{z=1}^{Z}n^{(z)}\,\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}\big[\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)};\mathcal{D}^{(z)})\,\big|\,\mathcal{D}^{(-z)}\big]\right]

It therefore suffices to show that

𝔼⁡[J^​(πe,𝜶^(z),𝒟(z))|𝒟(−z)]=J⁡(πe),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)};\mathcal{D}^{(z)})\big|\mathcal{D}^{(-z)}\big]=J(\pi_{e}),

for each fold zz. To see this, let 𝐰^(z)\hat{\mathbf{w}}^{(z)} be defined by

w^i(z)​(s,a,r)≔α^i(z)​πi​(a|s)πe​(a|s)+ni(z)​πi​(a|s)∑j=1Knj(z)​πj​(a|s)​(r−∑k=1Kα^k(z)​πk​(a|s)πe​(a|s))\displaystyle\hat{w}_{i}^{(z)}(s,a,r)\coloneq\frac{\hat{\alpha}_{i}^{(z)}\pi_{i}(a|s)}{\pi_{e}(a|s)}+\frac{n_{i}^{(z)}\pi_{i}(a|s)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}n_{j}^{(z)}\pi_{j}(a|s)}\left(r-\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\hat{\alpha}_{k}^{(z)}\pi_{k}(a|s)}{\pi_{e}(a|s)}\right)

Then, conditional on 𝜶^(z)\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)}, these weights satisfy the normalization condition ∑i=1Kw^i(z)​(s,a,r)=r\sum_{i=1}^{K}\hat{w}_{i}^{(z)}(s,a,r)=r and the dominance condition πi​(a|s)=0⟹w^i(z)​(s,a,r)=0\pi_{i}(a|s)=0\implies\hat{w}_{i}^{(z)}(s,a,r)=0.

Moreover, J^​(πe,𝜶^(z),𝒟(z))\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)};\mathcal{D}^{(z)}) in (3.4) can be rewritten in the canonical generalized weighted-IPS form (3.1), with 𝐰^(z)\hat{\mathbf{w}}^{(z)} as its weights:

J^​(πe,𝜶^(z),𝒟(z))=∑i=1K1ni(z)​∑(S,A,R)∈𝒟i(z)w^i(z)​(S,A,R)​πe​(A∣S)πi​(A∣S).\displaystyle\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)};\mathcal{D}^{(z)})=\sum_{i=1}^{K}\frac{1}{n_{i}^{(z)}}\sum_{(S,A,R)\in\mathcal{D}_{i}^{(z)}}\hat{w}_{i}^{(z)}(S,A,R)\,\frac{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{i}(A\mid S)}.

Since 𝐰^(z)\hat{\mathbf{w}}^{(z)} satisfies the normalization and dominance conditions conditional on 𝜶^(z)\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)}, Theorem 3.1 implies that J^​(πe,𝜶^(z),𝒟(z))\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)};\mathcal{D}^{(z)}) is unbiased conditional on 𝜶^(z)\hat{\bm{\alpha}}^{(z)}, equivalently conditional on 𝒟(−z)\mathcal{D}^{(-z)}.

Asymptotic Normality.

Next, we show that

n′​(J^oIPS​(πe,𝒟)−J⁡(πe))​→𝑑​𝒩​(0,n​Var​[J^​(πe,𝐰⋆,𝒟)]).\displaystyle\sqrt{n^{\prime}}\left(\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}(\pi_{e};\mathcal{D})-J(\pi_{e})\right)\overset{d}{\to}\mathcal{N}\left(0,n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\mathbf{w}^{\star};\mathcal{D})]\right).

We work with known logging policies under Assumption 1: KK and ZZ are fixed, the logger-wise folds are balanced up to rounding, the fitted scores converge in probability to the oracle score in each L2​(μπi)L^{2}(\mu_{\pi_{i}}), and all fitted and oracle scores have finite second moments, including over training randomness.

We rewrite our infeasible optimal estimator J^​(πe,𝜶⋆,𝒟)\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\bm{\alpha}^{\star};\mathcal{D}) in (3.4) in the form considered by Kallus et al. [2021]:

J^​(πe,𝜶⋆,𝒟)=1n​∑i=1K∑(S,A,R)∈𝒟i[πe​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S)​(R−g𝜶⋆πe​(S,A))+g𝜶⋆πe​(S,πe)].\displaystyle\hat{J}(\pi_{e},\bm{\alpha}^{\star};\mathcal{D})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\sum_{(S,A,R)\in\mathcal{D}_{i}}\left[\frac{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}\left(R-\frac{g_{\bm{\alpha}^{\star}}}{\pi_{e}}(S,A)\right)+\frac{g_{\bm{\alpha}^{\star}}}{\pi_{e}}(S,\pi_{e})\right].

The normal equation gives the oracle summand mean J⁡(πe)J(\pi_{e}) under every logger. Grouping the oracle observations into mm independent blocks, each containing nin_{i} observations from logger ii, the i.i.d. central limit theorem gives the displayed limit.

Conditional independence and the assumed L2L^{2} score convergence make each fold’s contribution to the centered error relative to the oracle, scaled by n′\sqrt{n^{\prime}}, op​(1)o_{p}(1) by conditional Chebyshev. With known policies, the conditional bias is zero. Since ZZ is fixed and fold weights are sample proportions, summing the contributions and applying Slutsky’s theorem gives the desired asymptotic normality result. If the logging policies are instead estimated by normalized policies fitted on the training folds, with positive mixtures, the same argument applies whenever each fold mean has conditional bias op(n′−1/2)o_{p}(n^{\prime-1/2}); this is the condition in Remark 2, and it is not implied by n\sqrt{n}-consistency of the estimated propensities. The same argument applies to DR scores under the corresponding moment, score-convergence, and bias conditions. ∎

E.4 Additional Proofs

Lemma E.2 (Normal-Equation Interpretation of 𝐓​𝜶=𝐜\mathbf{T}\bm{\alpha}=\mathbf{c}).

For 𝐓\mathbf{T} and 𝐜\mathbf{c} defined in (3.3), their entries can be written as

Ti​j=⟨πi,πj⟩μlog,ci=⟨q​πe,πi⟩μlog,\displaystyle T_{ij}=\big\langle\pi_{i},\pi_{j}\big\rangle_{\mu_{\log}},\quad c_{i}=\big\langle q\,\pi_{e},\pi_{i}\big\rangle_{\mu_{\log}},

where μlog\mu_{\log} is given by

d​μlogd​μs,a​(s,a)≔ps​(s)πavg​(s,a),\displaystyle\frac{d\mu_{\log}}{d\mu_{s,a}}(s,a)\coloneq\frac{p_{s}(s)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(s,a)},

with μs,a\mu_{s,a} denoting the base measure over 𝒮×𝒜\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}.

Consequently, 𝐓​𝛂=𝐜\mathbf{T}\bm{\alpha}=\mathbf{c} is the normal equation for the orthogonal projection of q​πeq\,\pi_{e} onto 𝒱≔span⁡({πi}i∈[K])\mathcal{V}\coloneq\mathrm{span}\big(\{\pi_{i}\}_{i\in[K]}\big). In particular, 𝐓​𝛂=𝐜\mathbf{T}\bm{\alpha}=\mathbf{c} admits a solution, and any solution 𝛂⋆\bm{\alpha}^{\star} defines the orthogonal projection of q​πeq\,\pi_{e} onto 𝒱\mathcal{V} through ∑i∈[K]αi⋆​πi\sum_{i\in[K]}\alpha_{i}^{\star}\pi_{i}.

Proof of Lemma E.2.

Recall the definitions of 𝐓\mathbf{T} and 𝐜\mathbf{c} in (3.3):

Ti​j≔𝔼μπi​[πj​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S)],ci≔𝔼μπi​[R​πe​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S)].\displaystyle T_{ij}\coloneq\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{i}}}\!\left[\frac{\pi_{j}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}\right],\ \ c_{i}\coloneq\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{i}}}\!\left[R\,\frac{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}\right].

The first identity follows by direct computation:

Ti​j\displaystyle T_{ij} =𝔼μπi​[πj​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{i}}}\!\left[\frac{\pi_{j}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}\right]
=∫Ωπi​(a|s)​πj​(a|s)πavg​(a|s)​pr​(r|s,a)​ps​(s)​𝑑μ​(ω)\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\frac{\pi_{i}(a|s)\pi_{j}(a|s)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(a|s)}\,p_{r}(r|s,a)\,p_{s}(s)\,d\mu(\omega)
=∫𝒮×𝒜πi​(a|s)​πj​(a|s)​ps​(s)πavg​(a|s)​d​μs,a​(s,a)\displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}}\pi_{i}(a|s)\,\pi_{j}(a|s)\,\frac{p_{s}(s)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(a|s)}\,d\mu_{s,a}(s,a)
=⟨πi,πj⟩μlog.\displaystyle=\big\langle\pi_{i},\pi_{j}\big\rangle_{\mu_{\log}}.

Similarly, for cic_{i}, we have

ci\displaystyle c_{i} =𝔼μπi​[R​πe​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{i}}}\!\left[R\,\frac{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}\right]
=𝔼μπi[𝔼μπi[Rπe​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S)|S,A]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{i}}}\!\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{i}}}\!\left[R\,\frac{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}\,\middle|\,S,A\right]\right]
=𝔼μπi[𝔼μπi[R|S,A]πe​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{i}}}\!\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{i}}}\!\left[R\,\middle|\,S,A\right]\,\frac{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}\right]
=𝔼μπi​[q⁡(S,A)​πe​(A∣S)πavg​(A∣S)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\pi_{i}}}\!\left[q(S,A)\,\frac{\pi_{e}(A\mid S)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(A\mid S)}\right]
=∫Ωq⁡(s,a)​πe​(a|s)​πi​(a|s)πavg​(a|s)​pr​(r|s,a)​ps​(s)​𝑑μ​(ω)\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}q(s,a)\,\frac{\pi_{e}(a|s)\,\pi_{i}(a|s)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(a|s)}\,p_{r}(r|s,a)\,p_{s}(s)\,d\mu(\omega)
=∫𝒮×𝒜q⁡(s,a)​πe​(a|s)​πi​(a|s)​ps​(s)πavg​(a|s)​d​μs,a​(s,a)\displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}}q(s,a)\,\pi_{e}(a|s)\,\pi_{i}(a|s)\frac{p_{s}(s)}{\pi_{\mathrm{avg}}(a|s)}\,d\mu_{s,a}(s,a)
=⟨q​πe,πi⟩μlog.\displaystyle=\big\langle q\,\pi_{e},\pi_{i}\big\rangle_{\mu_{\log}}.

It remains to show that 𝐓​𝜶=𝐜\mathbf{T}\bm{\alpha}=\mathbf{c} is the normal equation for the orthogonal projection. Let

𝒱≔span⁡({πi}i∈[K])⊂L2​(μlog).\displaystyle\mathcal{V}\coloneq\mathrm{span}\big(\{\pi_{i}\}_{i\in[K]}\big)\subset L^{2}(\mu_{\log}).

Since 𝒱\mathcal{V} is finite-dimensional, it is closed. Hence, the orthogonal projection of q​πeq\,\pi_{e} onto 𝒱\mathcal{V} exists. Write this projection as

g𝜶⋆≔∑k∈[K]αk⋆​πk.\displaystyle g_{\bm{\alpha}^{\star}}\coloneq\sum_{k\in[K]}\alpha_{k}^{\star}\pi_{k}.

By the identities proved above, this system is exactly 𝐓​𝜶⋆=𝐜\mathbf{T}\bm{\alpha}^{\star}=\mathbf{c}. Therefore, 𝐓​𝜶=𝐜\mathbf{T}\bm{\alpha}=\mathbf{c} admits a solution, and any solution 𝜶⋆\bm{\alpha}^{\star} defines the orthogonal projection of q​πeq\,\pi_{e} onto 𝒱\mathcal{V} through g𝜶⋆=∑i∈[K]αi⋆​πig_{\bm{\alpha}^{\star}}=\sum_{i\in[K]}\alpha_{i}^{\star}\pi_{i}. ∎

Appendix F Computational Complexity and Scalability

In this section, we analyze the computational complexity of J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}}, especially when the number of loggers is large (K≈100K\approx 100). Although restricted-optimal coefficients require solving a linear system with technique matrix 𝐓∈ℝK×K\mathbf{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times K}, we show both theoretically and empirically that the added cost is modest for practical KK. In this appendix, NN denotes the total sample size, written nn in the main text.

F.1 Theoretical Complexity Analysis

Computing J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} within cross-fitting has two main steps: (i) estimating the technique matrix 𝐓\mathbf{T} and contribution vector 𝐜\mathbf{c}, and (ii) solving for 𝜶=𝐓−1​𝐜\bm{\alpha}=\mathbf{T}^{-1}\mathbf{c} (or its pseudoinverse analogue).

  1. (i)

    Matrix construction: Constructing 𝐓\mathbf{T} aggregates propensity terms over NN samples and KK loggers, yielding O⁡(N​K)O(NK) complexity. This matches the dominant complexity class of balanced IPS (J^bIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{bIPS}}), which also computes aggregate propensity statistics (e.g., ∑knk​πk\sum_{k}n_{k}\pi_{k}) per sample.

  2. (ii)

    Linear solve / pseudoinversion: Solving 𝐓​𝜶=𝐜\mathbf{T}\bm{\alpha}=\mathbf{c} has worst-case complexity O⁡(K3)O(K^{3}) with standard dense linear algebra (e.g., LU or SVD).

The total time is O⁡(Z⁡(N​K+K3))O(Z(NK+K^{3})), which is O⁡(N​K+K3)O(NK+K^{3}) for fixed ZZ. Accumulating the per-fold moments in one pass uses O⁡(Z​K2)O(ZK^{2}) additional memory, while storing all cross-logger propensities uses O⁡(N​K)O(NK). These counts exclude fitting nuisance models such as propensity models. We compute 𝜶\bm{\alpha} with the SVD-based Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse, which also handles a rank-deficient 𝐓\mathbf{T}; this occurs in the runtime study below, where all loggers are mixtures of the deterministic and uniform policies.

F.2 Empirical Runtime Analysis

To validate practicality, we measured runtime on the Letter dataset (N=20,000N=20{,}000, 2626 actions) with K=10K=10 and K=100K=100 loggers. Experiments ran on an Apple MacBook Air M1 (base model, 8GB RAM). Logging policies were generated by mixing the deterministic policy with a uniform policy. We compared Naive IPS, Balanced IPS, Weighted IPS [Agarwal et al., 2017], and our Optimal IPS. Methods requiring sample-dependent weights (Weighted IPS and Optimal IPS) used Z=5Z=5 cross-fitting folds.

Table 3 reports mean inference time per trial (milliseconds) over 200 independent runs. Each ±\pm value is the half-width of a 95%95\% confidence interval based on the normal approximation.

Observations.

  • •

    Scalability: Even at K=100K=100, Optimal IPS takes about 20ms per trial. This is slower than heuristic balanced IPS but still inexpensive for offline evaluation.

  • •

    Comparison with Weighted IPS: Runtime is comparable to Weighted IPS. This is expected because both methods use cross-fitting and dataset passes to estimate nuisance quantities (variance terms for Weighted IPS, technique matrix for Optimal IPS). The linear solve adds limited overhead relative to those passes.

  • •

    Efficiency–Compute Trade-off: For a small runtime increase (milliseconds), Optimal IPS reduces Relative-RMSE by about 40%40\% versus Weighted IPS and about 48%48\% versus Balanced IPS in the K=100K=100 setting.

Practical Takeaway.

These numbers should be interpreted in the context of the full OPE pipeline. In our runs, end-to-end processing, including data loading, preprocessing, and fitting logger models, dominates total cost. Against that baseline, the additional time for J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} remains a moderate fraction of wall-clock time rather than a bottleneck, while providing substantial accuracy gains.

F.3 Large-NN Synthetic Experiment

We use the synthetic data generator of the Open Bandit Pipeline (OBP, version 0.5.7) [Saito et al., 2021] with 1010 actions, five-dimensional Gaussian contexts, and binary rewards from a logistic model with fixed coefficients. The evaluation policy chooses the action with the highest conditional mean reward. Each of the five known logging policies mixes the evaluation policy with the uniform policy, with uniform-exploration probabilities 0.050.05, 0.250.25, 0.500.50, 0.750.75, and 0.950.95, and all strata have the same size. For each N∈{104,105,106}N\in\{10^{4},10^{5},10^{6}\}, we draw contexts, actions, and rewards with 2020 independent random seeds. The ground-truth value is the evaluation policy’s conditional mean reward averaged over the sampled contexts. Weighted IPS and J^oIPS\hat{J}_{\mathrm{oIPS}} use five-fold cross-fitting. Confidence intervals are computed as in §5, with the 2020 seeds as the resampled units.

We ran these measurements on an x86-64 Linux machine with eight allocated CPU cores and 1212 GiB of RAM. Runtimes exclude data generation and the computation of propensities; peak memory includes the stored cross-logger propensities.

Appendix G Related Work

OPE evaluates counterfactual policies from logged data [Precup et al., 2000, Bottou et al., 2013]. Although classical treatments focus on a single logger, many real applications aggregate data from multiple behavior policies, such as parallel A/B systems, leading to a stratified design in which logger identity defines strata [Agarwal et al., 2017, He et al., 2019, Kallus et al., 2021, Chen et al., 2020, Wooldridge, 2001].

OPE with Multiple Loggers.

Agarwal et al. [2017] initiated the multi-logger OPE literature with MIS-inspired IPS estimators [Veach and Guibas, 1995, Cornuet et al., 2012, Elvira et al., 2019] and showed that no single estimator uniformly dominates across instances. Kallus et al. [2021] formalized this setting, derived the semiparametric efficiency bound, and proposed doubly robust estimators that asymptotically attain it. Related directions include off-policy learning with multiple loggers [He et al., 2019], infinite-horizon analysis [Chen et al., 2020], and generalization under selection bias [Hatt et al., 2022]. Liu et al. [2025] studied multi-policy evaluation in RL via behavior-policy design.

Multiple Importance Sampling.

MIS was originally developed to combine multiple proposal distributions in Monte Carlo rendering [Veach and Guibas, 1995, Owen and Zhou, 2000, Elvira et al., 2019, Kondapaneni et al., 2019]. The balance and power heuristics [Veach and Guibas, 1995] provide robust performance under nonnegative weights, and later work studied broader weighting families [Elvira et al., 2019]. Kondapaneni et al. [2019] derived variance-optimal MIS weights that may be negative, yielding further variance reduction in some regimes. Our method adapts this variance-minimization perspective to multi-logger OPE.

Broader Context.

Beyond the multi-logger setting, there is extensive work on variance control for IPS in standard OPE. Classical IPS traces back to Horvitz–Thompson [Horvitz and Thompson, 1952]. Subsequent work studied weight truncation [Ionides, 2008] and doubly robust estimation in contextual bandits [Dudík et al., 2014]. More recent lines include self-normalization and implicit-exploration objectives [Swaminathan and Joachims, 2015, Kuzborskij et al., 2021], transformations yielding sub-Gaussian concentration [Metelli et al., 2021], and pessimistic regularization through PAC-Bayesian analysis [Aouali et al., 2024]. These methods are complementary to, rather than replacements for, our multi-logger focus.

Appendix H Broader Impacts

This work is methodological research on off-policy evaluation with multiple logging policies. Its main positive impact is to make retrospective policy evaluation more reliable in domains where direct online testing may be costly or risky, such as recommender systems, healthcare decision support, and advertising. The main potential negative impacts arise from downstream use: more accurate OPE could still be used to justify the deployment of policies trained on biased, privacy-sensitive, or otherwise unrepresentative logs, and an incorrectly specified evaluation pipeline could give false confidence in a harmful policy. These risks are not unique to our estimator, but they motivate using it together with domain review, data-governance checks, privacy controls, fairness and subgroup analyses, and prospective validation before deployment in high-stakes settings.
